utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following yesterday's discussion on procedure --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked for the witness to be kept out briefly because following yesterday's discussion on procedure, we researched the law to see if there was any guidance of assistance. There's quite a number of first instance decisions which go several -- which go both ways. There are arguably two decisions in the Appeals Chamber of assistance; one the Appeals Chamber from the ICTR, one the Appeals Chamber from the ICTY, and one decision at first instance that we would like to draw to your attention. I'm happy to deal with it now or, depending on what plans the Chamber had made for dealing with the documents we looked at yesterday, at a later stage. If we deal with it now, having printed copies or extracts from the three judgements and there are only three short passages, one in each judgement to be referred to, those copies aren't yet with us but we -- they are with us, and alternatively, we can deal with it rapidly by putting it on the overhead projector. So I'm in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer will you be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not very much. I would hope to finish in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear the evidence. We'll hear the evidence without making any decision on those evidential points. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to tell you the following: Since in relation to the question that you're discussing right now, Mr. Nice yesterday mentioned a few persons who played an active role in this context, and he asked Mr. Balevic about them. One of these persons, perhaps the most prominent one among them that Mr. Nice mentioned yesterday is Kosta Bulatovic, and I wish to inform you that Kosta Bulatovic is on the witness list. He is on the list of witnesses. So you will have an opportunity of hearing his testimony. Therefore, I think that this is pointless to ask someone about statements given to the press, what the newspapers wrote about ages ago. I'm not going to use the word "group." I'm not going to say "among this group," but -- because I don't think there was a group, but among these activists, he was perhaps the most prominent one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I need not remind you, Mr. Milosevic, it's a strategy that you yourself employed at times in cross-examination, but we have to determine the issue. Let us hear the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to hear Kosta Bulatovic is going to come. It will probably help me tailor the questions I'm going to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's being done, as a matter of detail, we're still awaiting a prospective forthcoming witness list. I hope it's going to be with us shortly because planning is becoming a little tricky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you will take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, some questions that may be answered and dealt with very briefly, just yes or no: Following the demonstrations by students in 1981, were you aware of, did you ever read the petition that the students submitted in respect of the punishments that had been meted out to them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In January 1986, there was a petition signed by many Serbs complaining of the position, and it's a petition that relates to the activity of the group of people we've been discussing. Did you -- you didn't sign the petition. Did you see the petition yourself ever?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, those matters can be dealt with by the other witness, and I shan't even attempt to deal with them through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us -- and I'm afraid because of a slight change of plan I may not have organised Ms. Dicklich's assistance in the way that I ordinarily would have done, but you told us yesterday that you attended the one demonstration in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me one minute. Your Honours, can I save time? Lay on the overhead projector --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I save time? Lay on the overhead projector a printout from The Independent newspaper via a website from the 26th of September, 1998. And it's in English. We see the first page showing the date. If we could have the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The press reported, Mr. Balevic, on the rally in Nis as follows: "Saturday's rally in the south Serbian city of Nis involved some 150.000 people, according to unbiased accounts, and was one of the largest demonstrations seen in Yugoslavia. Those most outspokenly critical of the rallies, like the leaders of the prosperous Western Republic of Slovenia were, as is now routine, branded as supporters of the 'separatists and counter-revolutionaries' allegedly holding sway in Kosovo. 'For a tomorrow without those who destroyed yesterday,' said one banner." Now, was the demonstration in which you participated in Nis as large as 150.000 people?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I was in Nis at the rally where President Slobodan Milosevic spoke. As for what you've been saying, I don't know anything about that. These were not demonstrations. This was a rally, as far as I'm concerned. Demonstrations are when people walk down a street, get engaged in destruction, and so on. Mr. Milosevic spoke there and there was no incident whatsoever. What you say about Slovenia and the Slovenian leaders, for Slovenia, Kosovo and Metohija was a marginal matter. It was completely on the sidelines. They were not interested in it at all, the situation there and the drama of the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo. As a matter of fact, they supported Albanian separatism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me make an observation at this stage because it may be of relevance to the later debate, and I don't want to lose sight of it. You had a very simple question there about how many people were at the rally. That question, in my opinion, did not require this document to be read, and by reading the document you rather inflamed the witness to respond to all the various things in there about which inevitably he doesn't agree, and I don't think that that is a very productive way of cross-examining a witness like this. And it does raise questions, I think, over the value of using this kind of documentation in the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a comment for the moment so that we don't waste -- and please ignore it and continue to examine as you consider appropriate, but it's so that you have it in mind when we come to the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, and of course I put the document in because it deals with other matters, and one of them I do wish to ask the witness about. As to the 150.000 people, I haven't had an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But help us, please, with this, Mr. Balevic: Was Mr. Solevic with you at the time of this rally?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that rally, when I came there, I didn't see Mr. Solevic. There was a rally before that in Nis, though. I was at the rally where Slobodan Milosevic spoke, and I cannot say that there were 150.000 people there. It was held in front of the theatre, and I don't think that that area can really receive 150.000 people. So I cannot claim that. As for Solevic, I did not see him at the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you at about this time in contact with Solevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we may come back to this topic with the other witness who is going to be able to deal with it. The particular passage I was interested in but in light of His Honour Judge Bonomy's observation won't pursue is at the foot of this page. I don't think you can actually see it on the overhead projector, we'll come back to it later, but there was an integrated purpose in looking at this document as normally when I'm looking at documents of this kind. Can we move on, then, please, and I forecast that this will be on the same basis as -- if at all, as production of the documents yesterday, to look at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get a copy of this Independent article that Mr. Nice quoted from a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And indeed the last paragraph on the page to which I was going to refer is something that might qualify on one reckoning as Rule 68 material, which is one of the reasons I was going to draw it to the attention of the Court. So it's available for the accused to raise in re-examination. If he chooses to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now, please, on the same basis I would forecast, if at all, look at some extracts from The Death of Yugoslavia film which are stripped of all commentary and cover the build-up to and the events at the meeting on April 1987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you hoping to extract from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm hoping to extract from the witness that he agrees with many of the things that are said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we have the extracts. And the blank pages that Your Honours will see reflect editorial commentary that has now been excised so that all that you're left with is the words of the individual participants speaking to the commentator, I think, if anything else. The way it's being presented by Ms. Dicklich makes it possible for us to pause within the clip, as we will describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before we start, you told us, Mr. Balevic, of the visit that was planned -- sorry, the visit that was made by President Stambolic the year before, in 1986, a visit that was not regarded as successful by the Kosovo Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. As a form of protest, they left when he was making this speech in front of the Braca Krajinovic hall, because before that, a meeting was held inside where he spoke. But they were dissatisfied with his speech - there were a few thousand citizens in front of the building - so they left in protest because they expected Ivan Stambolic to say there which measures he's going to take as president within the scope of his authority in the Republic of Serbia and in Yugoslavia in order to stop the moving out of Serbs and Montenegrins and to ensure their safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If Ms. Dicklich could start the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of detail, I think we see you standing beside the accused on the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the man Solevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me where I am? You said that I was standing next to Slobodan Milosevic. I would only be too pleased to be standing next to him. But where am I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the Sanction and the monitor of the video shows different things. Yes. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'd better go back to the beginning, Your Honour. Ms. Dicklich will play her clip and I hope we're all seeing it. I will forget the point about standing next door and we'll just get on -- oh, here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pausing there, is that you standing beside Mr. Milosevic or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the next section.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 20th of April, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the man Solevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Solevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Play it, please. I must check that the -- pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is Mr. Solevic correct in saying that the accused had no initial intention of meeting the Serbs, on your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement of his is not correct. If it pertains to Mr. Milosevic, that is. Or do you mean Ivan Stambolic? Could you please tell me very specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the accused. So you say that from the very first day he was willing to come and speak to you? He didn't have to be compelled?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following: From the 16th of April, when I informed him and I invited him to come to a meeting, that is what I can talk about. I don't know what his feelings were before that. I do not recall any of that. I first spoke to him on the 16th of April, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is what we've been looking at the accused speaking on the first visit on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image is blurred, so I cannot even confirm where it is that he's speaking. You can see the school here. The school is opposite -- or, rather, he was speaking from a place that was opposite the school. So I cannot confirm the venue. I have to add one more thing, though. The rally in Nis, I think, was dedicated to a particular anniversary, so it was not a rally like the ones that were held before that, as far as I can remember, and I think that my memory serves me well. I cannot confirm where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really tell from this picture because I can't see the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we don't have voice here, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. He has the voice. I hope he has the voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, were you able to hear the sound in this clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We understood that the sound was going to the witness. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but I can't hear this. I can just see the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's better. Pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. Balevic, you heard that. Is it right, as Solevic says, that the accused was invited to return on the basis --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't remember this, this contact between Solevic and Milosevic. I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that at certainly the first meeting and even at the second the accused stuck to the traditional brotherhood and unity line?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the usual line. It was his policy, his official policy in favour of brotherhood and unity of the peoples in Kosovo. It was not the usual line, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Pause there. The next bit couldn't be cut, Your Honours, without cutting out Borisav Jovic's comment. We will pass through it quickly when we reactivate the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But tell me this, please, Mr. Balevic: We hear there Mr. Jovic saying that the first person to stand up and to say we must stop the oppression of the Serbs had the way to the top. Was that your understanding, that the accused, by supporting those who were complaining of oppression of the Serbs, made for himself a way to the top?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He confirmed this course because he placed himself at the helm of the massive request from Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija for their very survival. It wasn't any kind of leadership. It's not that Milosevic called us. We called him to come to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We'll advance through the somewhat realistic beheading and get to the next passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is Dusan Mitrovic, now dead. He died shortly after of, I think, cancer. And he was the deputy head of Belgrade television; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I never had any contact with him. I don't know. I know he was on television, but otherwise I had no contacts with him at all, nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is Azem Vllasi, communist leader at the time until he was removed from office and imprisoned, correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of the provincial committee. He was a Tito youngster. And unfortunately, later on he toppled the state that Tito had created. And he was a Tito person in his youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember yesterday that I asked you whether between the first and second meeting there was any contacts between the accused and those of you down in Kosovo? And I'd like you to listen to the following with that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seeing those two passages, is there any reason to doubt that the accused may have sent someone down between the first and second meetings to arrange what was to happen?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of him having sent anybody there between the first and second meeting. I had nothing to do with him, no contacts with him between the first and second meeting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You -- you were a --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. But the first meeting was a rally. The second was a meeting held in a closed room. So there are not two rallies, just one meeting, one of which was held behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've made a point of the fact that you're not one of the group itself, even if you once went with some members of the group to see Dizdarevic. Do you exclude the possibility or do you allow for the possibility that the accused may indeed have sent somebody down to deal with people such as Solevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, nobody from that group with us went to see Dizdarevic, but I allow for the fact that you might wish to check it out. As far as I remember and as far as my memory serves me, that's how it was, because yesterday I used this as a reminder, as an aide-memoire, and I was cautioned by Mr. Robinson that I was reading. I wasn't actually reading, I just used it to refresh my memory. But as I say, I myself don't remember that anybody from the group was there with us when we went to see Dizdarevic, and I have been repeating this several times, that is that I did not belong to that group myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with that in a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should just like to draw your attention to this: I am listening to what these various individuals here are saying and I can see the translation at the bottom, and let me tell you that the translation is not very correct. Vllasi, speaking in Albanian, says that Milosevic sent the executive secretary. I can hear him saying this in Albanian, "ekzekutiv sekretar," "executive secretary." And I assume that "ekzekutiv" means "executive" in Albanian too. And then the translation said, or the caption said, "He sent a private secretary." I didn't have a private secretary. I had a lady secretary. Now, what Vllasi says should at least be translated from the Albanian to English correctly, just as one should translate correctly what is said in Serbian by others in the captions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is this intended to be a faithful translation or paraphrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the translation that's provided by the company that made the tapes. May I propose that we run the tape, not now but afterwards, through another -- with other translators and it can be given an authoritative translation in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We take account of the point made by Mr. Milosevic, but you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Example, Mr. Robinson. For example, there we have an example. Solevic here is explaining that they had brought in some material to expand the pavement, and I just heard him say and Mr. Balevic heard him say that and anybody else who was listening. He said that was brought in to expand and broaden the pavement. It wasn't intended for the police. That's what he is explaining, but you can't see that in the translation. In the translation, there's just an abridged version, a hodgepodge of what was said, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we may be obliged to consider adopting the course that you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as this point may be important, could we have it played -- run it again and let us have the interpreters translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter here in the Albanian booth cannot hear the Albanian. When he tries to speak into English, it gets cut off.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "[Previous translation continues]... have time. It's Friday, Monday. We have Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday to get ready. Just three days. Each of us going in our own way to meet people, to have a look -- to talk to them, to organise ourselves. We said all these lads who can fight properly should take everything they need. "MR. SOLEVIC: We unloaded two tractor trailers to broaden the pavement, yes, broaden the pavement. It wasn't for the police. It was just there in case. "SPEAKER: I want to live here where my mother lived. I want to be buried here in this soil where --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise but the speed of the tape is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just go back to the first passage. You saw what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard what Solevic said about parking lorries for broadening the pavement but just in case. Was it, as I suggested to you, the case that there were preparations made to generate a conflict to which the accused could respond?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. And I'm hearing about these lorries or trailers for the first time, and those bricks, and it's just not true. And secondly, I was in the hall, so I wasn't able to see what was going on outside, whether there are any stones or not, but this observation is incorrect, and this is the first time that I'm hearing it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that any kind of preparations were being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without translation for this passage. We've had this before in the accused's evidence, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the interpreters could interpret this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We don't know what was going on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Our people started fleeing, and this encouraged the police and they started running after us until we got to the -- they got to the stones and then we turned round. So everybody got a gift like that on their -- on the helmet. And then we went up to Milosevic again and said the police outside are beating our people and then he couldn't pass this hot potato to anybody else. He had to go out himself, and he was probably rather afraid and nervous because he knew what was going on and what this meant."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, Mr. Robinson, another example. You can hear here that they're saying to me, "They're beating us." And then you can hear my voice saying, "Nobody must be allowed to beat you," whereas the translation at the bottom of the caption says, "Nobody must beat you again." The word "again" doesn't exist anywhere. They say, "They're beating us," and I say, "Nobody must be allowed to beat you." That's all, and that's quite logical. It goes -- it follows on one from the other. Now, who added the word "again," you will have to ask your employees about that or, rather, Mr. Nice over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The matter we discussed yesterday. I'm grateful for the observation and it doesn't come, I think, entirely as a surprise. Can we move on, just get to the end of the clip, and then I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that bit translated?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise but they cannot translate from the tape. It's much too fast and indistinct except for bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreters, did they not hear the "You will not be beaten?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We heard the "You will not be beaten," yes, but I can't guarantee for any other sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was there any "again" in that sentence? I'm asking the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just on to the end, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to ask the interpreters, would you have the video played again from the point where Mr. Milosevic came out, and I'd like them to attend as closely as possible to the -- that part of his speech concerning beating, I think on two occasions. If we could have as close a translation as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As far as the interpreter heard, there was no "again" on both occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can press on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, having looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, having looked at those observations by the people who we know, I come again to the question: Was there not at this meeting an element of planning in order to give the accused an opportunity to lead the Serbs who were making complaint at the meeting you'd organised?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say with full responsibility that it is the first time that I'm hearing Solevic here and now talking about some construction work and preparations for construction work and bringing in material to place an asphalt layer on a road. So this construction material and bricks I can say with full responsibility I never saw, and I heard it for the first time here. No preparations were conducted -- and I have to state once again, Mr. Milosevic, when he came out on two occasions, because I was standing next to him, and as far as I heard him, the first time he said, "Nobody must be allowed to beat you." And the second time, "Nobody must beat." And then Miodrag Trifovic, who is the son, the grey-haired man, he is the uncle of Dragan Trifovic who was killed in the Panda cafe, and he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I understand clearly what you're putting to the witness. You're saying that this was planned cynically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cynically. So the accused could emerge as a leader. And in this melee people would be injured. Are you saying that all that was planned? Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment and until if he comes as a witness, he comes as a witness, or if they come as witnesses in due course, I'm dependent on material both from the words of Solevic, which are amplified in considerable detail in what he says in other parts of the complete interview, which can be made available, and I'm dependent on the words of Vllasi, also contained in the full interview and in other texts, which would suggest that there was certainly an element of planning between the two meetings and quite possibly an element of planning before the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, not just planning. Your case is not just that there was planning for the meeting but planning in such a way that there would be a disturbance in which people might be injured and out of which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the accused would emerge as a leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is the clear effect of what Solevic is saying, and that is a possibility that indeed we are countenancing, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solevic doesn't say that at all. What Mr. Nice is claiming, Solevic did not say at all. He just thought it up, just as he thought up the planning of a joint enterprise. That's his speciality. And it's a great shame here that he is operating with things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you'll have a time to make comments when you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to make my position absolutely clear through a question I've asked before of the witness but I'll now ask again, in light of His Honour Judge Robinson's concern and arising from things that Solevic has said specifically, do you have any knowledge, Mr. Balevic, of strong young Serb men armed with pistols being arranged to be present in the crowd on that occasion to turn to violence if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that kind at all. I claim that that is incorrect, that it was all construed and staged in order to proclaim the meeting, the rally, or, rather, to create incidents breaking out and to lead to chaos. So that observation in your question to me is incorrect, and you're basing it on Solevic and Vllasi whereas I'm basing my testimony on the facts that I saw and were able to follow, and I'm not basing it on Solevic and Vllasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Unless Solevic ever attends as a witness here, can you think of any reason why Solevic, from whom you parted company later in 1998, or separated generally, can you think of any reason why he should make such things up, so we can know it now?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what year we parted ways ideologically. We didn't see eye-to-eye. But I think it would be a good idea if you were to ask him to come here and then he would be able to tell you about those ideas and the statements, because I don't know what his ideas were and what his statements meant. I cannot interpret them. The best thing would be for him to tell you here from this seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you tell us why Mr. Solevic was not in the witness list in Kosovo case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were a number of people who might have been on the witness list but of course we didn't call for all sorts of reasons. I don't know that Solevic was even available to us at that time or whether he will be available to us now. I can make efforts now. But at that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you were aware of this film at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we were certainly aware of the film at that time, but our efforts at that time, I think, were concentrated on other witnesses like, for example, Vllasi, and we didn't go to this witness at that time, no. But those are the choices that one makes, and sometimes witnesses become more obviously relevant and valuable at a later stage, and it's the broadening of the -- it's the broadening of the case by the accused in relation to this meeting that makes this particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This concept of an accused broadening his case is new to me. The accused has a right to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to put his Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no objection to it at all, as I've made absolutely clear. I don't object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a definitional contradiction [Realtime transcript read in error "definition contradiction"].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The accused can't broaden his case, he puts his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He puts his case and he puts it in a particular way, it may have the effect of broadening the matters into which we have to look in detail. We presented evidence about this meeting in a fairly narrow way. It's now wider, and that's why we're looking into it. Your Honours, with your leave, may I move on to something that the witness will want we to deal with. I was going to overlook it, although I've referred to it, but in light of his question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just saw something here. I said it's a definitional contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And since what I want to put to the witness is arguably favourable to the witness as well, and since he's raised it, I'd better put it although it was going to be something I was going to cut to save time. Can he have, please, an extract from Raif Dizdarevic's book which deals with the meeting, he having questioned the composition of the group that went to see Dizdarevic, who is, I think, still alive but elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, this is the passage I referred to right at the beginning of my cross-examination of you where you're described as moderate or moderate in comparison. You've asked me about the composition of the meeting as reflected in the book and that's why I'm taking the time to deal with it. You'll see on the first page -- if Mr. Prendergast could put it on, the first page, on the overhead projector. "Late at night on the 24th of February, Petar Gracanin called me on the telephone. He said that a delegation of Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo were in Belgrade. They had come in a serious and representative composition and asked to talk to me and at the General Staff. I said that those in Serbia talk to them and see what this was all about, and only after that information, I would give my answer. After awhile, he called me again and asked me to see the delegation. The situation in Kosovo, he said, was dramatic and they were all asking to talk to me. Also he himself asked me that and the leadership of Serbia as well. After that I saw the delegation at around midnight and spoke with them for more than two hours in the presence of Gracanin. It was led by Balevic, a party official from Kosovo Polje, who at the time was known as a moderate liner in comparison with Solevic, Kecman and other extremists from Kosovo. "To my question, 'Why are there no Albanians among you?' Balevic answered that 'At this time it is hard to be together.' "They told me the reasons for their arrival." So you see, the way that Dizdarevic sets out the meeting, Mr. Balevic, he doesn't identify beyond giving your name, I think, the composition of the group. Do you see?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have complicated things here. It's true that I was a moderate. It is true that we asked to familiarise him with the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. When he says more moderate than Solevic and others, he doesn't claim that Solevic was at that meeting. Please read the whole list and tell me, where does it say that Solevic went to see Dizdarevic. As far as I know, he didn't. But he had some background information, and on the basis of that he decided that I was more moderate than Solevic. However, as to the composition of the group, you can read Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the list and find out who was there and who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The point is the list isn't there, which is why I'm drawing it to your attention. Having seen that passage of what he says, and we can see the rest of the summary of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will find it in Dizdarevic's protocol service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- for want of time I'm happy for the document to be exhibited. I'm happy for it to fulfil any other function, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the question simply whether the witness was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a question whether he was there, whether he's in a position now that he's seen, because he asked us to say how it was recorded, whether he's in a position now to help us further with the composition of that meeting, because the group of people to whom I've been referring is Solevic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Balevic, can you help us further? Look at the detail or the record of the meeting if it's going to prompt your memory. Can you help us further with whom you went to as the head of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you all the people who was there. There was myself, Djuro Bauk, Ljubo Vujevic. I don't know else was there. It was a long time ago. We acquainted Dizdarevic first with a message sent to him by Gracanin about the dramatic situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and it was really dramatic because 10.000 people were waiting outside in the street for us to come back and report to them. And I underline one of those who spoke, Ljubo Vujovic, asked Dizdarevic how long would it take the army to get out of the barracks and intervene, and he replied, "I believe three or four hours." And our response was, "If it's anything more than 15 minutes, it will be too late."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other reason I wanted the witness to have on balance an opportunity to look at this is because I said at the beginning that he'd once been described as more moderate and in the circumstances of the challenges I'm making to him it seemed fair that he should see where I derived that from. Can we move on, and Your Honours, can I explain what I'm going to do. The witness has given some observations about matters of demography. I understand from the accused's proposed witness list that he's going to call a demographer himself, and there's still the outstanding issue of the demographic evidence that was cut off at the time of the conclusion of the Prosecution's case, so I shall deal with matters of demography through experts rather than with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: However, there's one matter of detail that you can assist us with, please, Mr. Balevic. You've spoken of a place called Klina, which is hard for us to find. Does it have an another name, Glina? Is it the same as the place Glina?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right, that's all I need.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not the same thing. Glina is somewhere in Bosnia and Croatia or wherever it is. Klina is in Kosovo and Metohija, near Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Near Pec. We'll see if we can find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close to Pec, about 20 -- Pec is to the north -- sorry, to the west of Klina, towards Montenegro, and Klina is about 25, 26 kilometres from Pec to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, please, to the speech at Gazimestan. You have been emphatic there was nothing nationalistic about what was happening at Gazimestan. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could see and observe, it is true. There was nothing nationalistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are a million Serbs in an area where Kosovo Albanians were clearly in a majority celebrating a Serb war. Do you think there's any risk of anxiety falling on the Kosovo Albanians in having a meeting of that scale in their -- in territory that they dominated?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it imposed a risk. It was a celebration of the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle, and the estimates of the press as to the number of people attending ran between 500.000 and a million. Those are not my estimates, and I don't think it could have been a risk. It would have been more of a risk to organise destructive demonstrations running through the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an event that was not designed to pose a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us of your handling the arrangements for such important guests as Ante Markovic and Drnovsek, whom I think you escorted in; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue what you're just saying, Mr. Nice. I never said I met Drnovsek or Markovic, unless it's blatant provocation, unless you're trying to provoke me. I was playing a host to those people coming by train, various people who came to take part in the event from various parts of the country, from Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't put words in my mouth, and I don't care for your apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But those men did come. You certainly told us about that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not welcome them. They were there, sitting in the first row, and I was behind them in the fourth row.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's look, please, with the assistance of the audiovisual booth at how this meeting ended. And perhaps you would be good enough, Mr. Balevic, to listen carefully to what we can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The words of the song that were sung in unison, "Ko To Kaze, Ko To Laze Srbija Je Mala," and so on, is as nationalistic a Serbian song as you can have, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this question. I was expecting it. First of all, Mr. Nice, it's not a nationalist song. It is a song that has been sung for a hundred years, back to the Balkan wars. It is sung at weddings, in taverns, at celebrations. It is an integral part of our folklore and this can be confirmed by ethnologists who are experts. That song was not sung only there, it has been sung every where, from the Balkan wars onwards. When you find two or three people gathering, making merry in a tavern, they will sing that song. It's not true that it's a nationalist song. If you allow me to tell you, although my knowledge of the Albanian language is poor by now, however, when I was young, I learnt it in school with my Albanian friends. If I -- if you allowed me to show you an example of an Albanian song, then you would see what nationalist means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is who sang that song.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've given a long answer. Now let's look at the words: "Who is saying, who is lying, that Serbia is small. It's not small, it's been to war three times, and it will be again if God grants us luck." Mr. Balevic, how do you think those words would have sounded in the ears of non-Serbs present at that meeting or non-Serbs from elsewhere in Yugoslavia hearing a million people singing it at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was not sung by a million people. It was sung by a part of those gathered but not a million. That's one thing. And second, regardless of all the slogans, that song is not nationalist by nature. I don't know how many times Serbia has been to war. Only one of those wars was silly, when King Milan attacked Bulgaria because of some silly ambitions. All the other wars, however, were national liberation wars. And that song does not mean that Serbia would go to war against Albanians. It's a hundred-year-old song, and if a hundred years ago it was -- it had the meaning you seem to impute to it, then all right. But what I'm saying is that it's part of our folklore, and it has been sung on various occasions over the past 100 years. You have, however, your own historians. You can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have shown some passing knowledge of the trials before this Tribunal, or certainly of this trial. Have you followed trials where Serbs are alleged to have -- the camp cases, for example, where Serbs are alleged to have done bad things to Croats and to Muslims, including making them sing nationalistic Serb songs? Have you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. After that song was sung, and indeed after the speech of the accused, you've told us about the arrival of Ante Markovic and Mr. Drnovsek. Did they in fact leave immediately?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that because I was not their escort.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. It is really inappropriate to manipulate with facts in this way. After this speech that Mr. Nice has just shown - in fact I showed the tape first - there followed a celebration, a cultural event, and there was even a piece of music composed specially for the occasion, and that was the 600th anniversary of the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's a matter you can take up in re-examination, as you well know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To move on and to explain how I'm going to save time, nevertheless trying to assist the Chamber with what matters are and are not in issue, the witness gave wide-ranging and, I assume from the way he described them, hearsay accounts of crimes committed by KLA. He referred to, I think, two or three places in particular; Lake Radonjic, Klecka, and one or two other places. These matters are already covered in evidence, for example, in Exhibit 191. I'm not going to challenge him as to detail, and indeed I think as to the generality without necessarily the atmosphere. His account of crimes by KLA is not challenged as to the generality but not necessarily as to the detail, we don't have time to go into that, but it probably helps for the Judges to -- for the Court to know why I'm not dealing with something even if I don't necessarily accept it as relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order to try and fulfil my hope and semi-promise of finishing this morning in the first session, you told us in relation to the build-up to the events of 1999, that you were at a meeting with the man Sainovic. Was it just the one meeting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's Sainovic who had a meeting with us at the provincial committee, and I personally never had a one-to-one meeting with Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I accept that. At the time -- at the time that you had your meeting with Sainovic, did he -- what position did he fulfill? What structure of control did he reflect?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall at the moment what position he was holding at the, but he came on behalf of the Main Staff of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he appear to have authority in some way over events in the area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he had any special powers. At least he didn't share it with us. But he often came to attend meetings of the Main Staff together with other leaders, Ruzica Gajevic, Milan Minic, Dragan Tomic, the other Dragan Tomic. I cannot recall all the people who attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you then or thereafter get an understanding of who was running things in Kosovo after the bombing began; who was the military commander for the Serbs, who was the civil commander? Did you get an understanding? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot help you there. I don't know who was the civilian commander or the military commander, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you get to learn of anybody called the Supreme Command; and if so, how it was composed?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Supreme Command, but I don't know who was on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you hear about it from?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that everybody knows in Serbia, that there is a Supreme Command, like in every state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In your evidence yesterday in answer to the accused, you said that there was no, to your knowledge, ethnic cleansing in Kosovo apart from that of Serbs and Montenegrins. And speaking of the columns of Albanians, you said this: That the columns of Albanians you came across were such that it didn't look to you as if they were refugee columns at all because they were going by slowly, past the railway station and the bus station, carrying small bags. They didn't look the way Serb columns looked. The columns looked to you to be sort of construed, manufactured, staged so that they should look like refugees. Is that really your evidence on what happened to the Kosovo Albanians in Pristina following the bombing in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I adhere to what I said yesterday, except I didn't say next to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. railway station, I said in the direction of the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you, please, to look with us at an exhibit. The number is Exhibit 15, already produced. It's on Sanction. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "People and its identity. The ethnic Albanians that once dominated this city are in flight. Forced from their homes, threatened and abused by the Serbian police, they are being herded into trains destined for the Macedonian border. They leave behind a country and a way of life which they may never see again. "The police came to our houses and told us to get out. They said they'd kill us if we didn't leave. They beat up my son. We've come here without money or possessions. "The border between Kosovo and Macedonia has become one vast and sprawling refugee camp. It could be a scene from the heart of Africa, but this is the heart of modern Europe. Tens of thousands are now here. Tens of thousands more ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first clip shows Pristina railway station, and the composition takes refugees to the border. Is what you saw at the railway station on the clip the sort of false, staged exodus that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said yesterday where this was happening. Whether it is the railway station of Pristina or some other railway station, I don't know. You cannot see the name of the station here. I have not been there. I spoke only about what I saw in Pristina, the people moving from the area of Dardanija towards the bus terminal and the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, Mr. Balevic, that your account of columns of Albanians looking like they were staging being refugees is unacceptable and simply false, that you're basically false in suggesting that these people were staging anything. You knew perfectly well that people were being forced out of Pristina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I equally reiterate that your statement is incorrect and that people were not driven out from Pristina by force. You cannot tell me that I'm saying something false. I am saying that you are not right. I'm speaking of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to consider one extract from Exhibit 145, already an exhibit in the case, on the overhead projector in English at page 137. This is Under Orders. Mr. Balevic, I'll read it to you slowly. This deals with the position at Pristina according to Human Rights Watch, and we'll see how they sourced their material, if necessary, from the footnotes. But the evidence is to this effect, or the book is to this effect, and the book is in evidence. Starting at the top of the page: "Police and masked paramilitaries went door-to-door at the end of March, telling residents that they had to leave at once. MB, a mother of two from Tashlixhe said that she had been told: 'Come on, get out, you must go to the railway station.' In come cases witnesses were told they would be killed if they failed to comply. A medical doctor and his family were told by masked men, 'If you don't leave in one minute, we will kill you all.'" And then this: "Upon leaving their homes, residents were directed by police towards the railway station in Pristina, while others left by car. The side roads were blocked by armed police and paramilitaries: A Vranjevac resident said that people who tried to walk in another direction were forced back by the police. Thousands of Pristina residents were gathered at the railway station, with armed police posted around the area ..." You were there. Is it your case that this account is true, false, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know absolutely nothing about this. I didn't go to Tashlixhe, that place is called Tashlixhe. I was in Dardanija, so I know nothing about this. You would have to find somewhere an article stating of Serbs and Montenegrins who were fleeing, because this particular publication was inclined towards separatists. And there were other publications of the same sort led by people by -- like Kandic, Biserko, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, you gave -- you were asked about ethnic cleansing, and you volunteered an answer which referred to the ethnic cleansing of Serbs and expressly or by implication said there was no ethnic cleansing of Kosovo Albanians from the area of which you had knowledge. Now I want you to help the Court, please, and we'll look at one more extract and then I'm done. We've looked at the document before. It's "As Seen, As Told" again, Exhibit 106, and you will remember, Mr. Balevic, that this was the document that we looked at yesterday where you found -- where we found together passages dealing with the KLA as well as with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Prendergast would put the page 236 on the overhead projector, right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is in Kosovo Polje. It's on the 29th of March. We can see it there. "Shots were fired --" Incidentally, it will help you if I set it in context although we don't have time. The previous passage deals entirely with what happened to a KLA leader, commander, and his family. Now we look at something different. "On the 29th of March, shots were fired at the house of a well known Kosovo Albanian doctor. VJ and police broke into the house, looted it and expelled the inhabitants. An interviewer who later entered the doctor's premises (his house and clinic combined) reported finding the bodies of 11 dead (two children, four women and five men). All had had their throats slit open. Only a four-year-old girl had survived this massacre." This is Kosovo Polje in the time before you left. Do you have any knowledge, were you ever told anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In light of your answer to the --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if I had any knowledge, I would share it with you. But what is interesting, Mr. Nice, is that you haven't asked me a single question relating to the tragedy experienced by the Serbs and Montenegrins, the murder in 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of people in Gacko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blowing up of buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You only take examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I answered the question. But Mr. Nice is picking out the sequences that only -- the kind that fits with the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a comment for you to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the whole point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I gave the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But more than that. You see, you gave an answer yesterday which effectively excluded suffering of Kosovo Albanians. They were either falsely pretending they were refugees, and they weren't killed or compelled in any way to leave the area. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, didn't the witness acknowledge yesterday that there were some misdeeds committed by Serbs, but they were malcontents, criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is quite right, he did. He acknowledged it to that extent to me in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this, as you'll see, Mr. Balevic, refers to the VJ, and it refers to the police. Do I take it from your answer that you say you don't know about it but that you allow for the fact that it may have happened?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not allow that possibility, because I know nothing of that. I'm not aware of that at all, and that's what I said yesterday. Apart from the examples I mentioned, which were exceptions, but that certainly did not constitute our policy, because I know all about the policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That concludes your cross-examination, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to take a break now for 20 minutes. Mr. Nice, would you let us have the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And it would probably help if I flag them for relevance, although of course we've included larger passages than the narrow ones so that you have context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you would have marked them, underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can do that, whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're to re-examine, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Balevic, yesterday when Mr. Nice started cross-examining, he spoke about dismissing Albanians from their jobs. I am going to quote paragraph 87 of the indictment where it says, inter alia: "Throughout the end of 1990 and throughout all of 1991, thousands of Kosovo Albanians -- Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police and civil servants were dismissed from their positions." Tell me, please, was anybody dismissing Albanians from their jobs because they were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, no. They left their jobs of their own free will. I said that yesterday, and I said that on the 25th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any campaign or any kind of organised activity aimed at dismissing Albanians from their jobs in your community?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing of that kind was done by official policy. This was done of their own accord. They left their jobs, and I underline this, in order to paint a certain picture before the international community, the international public, to show that this was this great injustice against them, and then whatever happened to Kosovo and Metohija was to follow. There was no campaign against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you why you used the word "Siptar." I don't know whether the explanation given was sufficiently clear. You lived in Kosovo for a long time. What is the word that Albanians use for themselves?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I give an explanation yesterday, and I claimed that that's the way it is. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your explanation. We heard it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the word that Albanians themselves use for themselves?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Siptari." They call themselves "Siptari." I claim that with full responsibility. They do not say "Albanians," they say "Siptari."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they know that too. Mr. Nice spoke to you then about some Serb positions and Albanian positions that differ. In the period of time that you are testifying about in relation to events in Kosovo, were these Serbian positions or generally accepted Yugoslav positions? When I say Yugoslav, I mean the presidents of Yugoslavia, the Yugoslav political leadership, the leaderships of the other socialist republics at the time. Were these positions espoused by all of them or were they some kind of separate Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, what positions are we talking about? Could you tell me please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Positions about the political situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these Serb positions exclusively or were these Yugoslav positions, positions espoused by the Yugoslav leadership?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not exclusively Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When mentioning the fact that they were readily admitted into university and readily given diplomas, you said by way of proof that a professor made a speech - Professor Milanovic was the name if I wrote it down correctly - at that gathering that you chaired. As for this inflation of diplomas, as it were, and this non-selective admission policy, in terms of individuals who were coming from Albania and were admitted at Pristina University, is that the only thing you know, what you heard from Milanovic that day at that particular meeting, or do you know more about that? Do you know that this was something that was discussed more widely in public?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Vujadin Milanovic. This is a well-known professor. I heard him speak and his speech is contained in this book and there is no need for me to read it out if this was admitted here anyway. Later on I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also heard about this and people were saying this is the way things were done. There is a lot more in this book, and what it says is far more serious than what I referred to yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're not going to read out from that book now but there are also stenographic notes from the meeting you chaired contained in that book; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I listened to the speech as it was being made because I was chairing the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nice said or, rather, he said he tried to establish the reasons why Serbs, as he said, wanted Albanians not to get an education. Was there ever a position like that taken by Serbs? When I say "Serbs," I'm referring to the public opinion, the leaderships in Kosovo, local leaderships, republican leaderships, Yugoslav leaderships. Did it cross anyone's mind to have that kind of motive, not to education the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that there was never such a motive or such a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that some group was sending delegations. Tell me, who was it that sent delegations? For example, to see Dizdarevic, who sent this delegation? You led that delegation. Who sent you on this delegation that went to see Dizdarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically we were sent by a group of 10 to 15.000 persons who were gathered before the Braca Krajinovic building in Kosovo Polje because they wanted to go to Belgrade, all of them. They asked for trains. And then we tried to stop that. We tried to prevent thousands of them going to Belgrade. We said that a delegation should be chosen, and these towns selected a delegation that went to see Dizdarevic in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the clip -- or, rather, in the excerpt from Raif Dizdarevic's book that Mr. Nice showed a few minutes ago, it says on page 365 - the one that he indicated, too, when he was quoting from it - that Petar Gracanin called him. Do you remember that at that time Petar Gracanin was president of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia after Ivan Stambolic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia, Petar Gracanin, called the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Raif Dizdarevic, and asked him to receive a delegation from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because first the chief of protocol called us, and he wanted to receive us. We didn't want to talk to the chief of protocol. We insisted that we talk to Dizdarevic himself. Then Petar Gracanin -- President Petar Gracanin intervened and then he received us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then this sentence that is being linked to this possible suspicion that Solevic was on the delegation with you and others, and I don't know what the point of this is even if he were. I'm going to read the sentence out. "The delegation was led by Balevic, a party official from Kosovo Polje who at that moment was considered to be a moderate compared to Solevic, Kecman, and other Kosovo extremists." Is that the truth as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what President Dizdarevic wanted to say by this. I did lead the delegation, but it's not that I was officially elected. They said, Since you are the president of the regional conference, you can head the delegation. He probably meant what was actually being said, because I actually tried to find a common solution with the Albanians through a more moderate policy. I guess that's the only way how he could have formed this opinion that I was moderate compared to Solevic and others. I don't know how else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Towards the end of this page, if you could please be so kind as to look at it, I'm just going to quote the last four or five lines. Dizdarevic says: "They asked not to accept Morina's, Azemi's and Shukrija's resignations. One of them said verbatim that if these resignations are accepted, then that would mean the resignation of Yugoslavia or the Albanisation of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the text so it is very hard to interpret this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 2 or 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have that text. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They should, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The text should be passed on to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think they do actually have text but they've probably been provided with a lot of material, hard to find.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The point is this; they requested the resignations of Morina, Azemi, and Shukrija not be accepted. Morina, Azemi, and Shukrija are Albanians. I believe that there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are a delegation and Mr. Nice asked you whether there were any Albanians on the delegation and you said no, there weren't any or, rather, he asked you -- or, rather, Dizdarevic asked you about this too. So this delegation didn't include any Albanians but you asked for support to be given to Morina, Azemi and Shukrija, that is so say the most prominent Albanian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mentioned, but Mr. President, how we actually put this into words is something I cannot say now. I think this was referred to. I think it was Rrahman Morina. I'm not sure about Azemi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He probably recorded it very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate your delegation asked for support to be given to Azemi, Shukrija and Morina.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all three Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dizdarevic referred to a plan --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, could we have the tape played from the part where Ivan Stambolic speaks and then I would like to put a question to Mr. Balevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the tape be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may need some identification of the clip. I forecast from the question that it's probably The Death of Yugoslavia tape, and if it's the one involving Mr. Stambolic, President Stambolic, then it will be the very beginning, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here in the transcript clip 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So Ivan Stambolic says that it was suggested to him that he should go to Milosevic but that he wanted me to go. Secondly, you testified here that you had invited me.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If he is asking me to go in both cases and you are inviting me, what kind of plan can I have, then, in relation to going to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No plan whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can play this clip in front of the cultural centre when this is coming to an end, when they say they are beating us and when I say no one should be allowed to beat you. And then the masses of people became more quiet. Did you notice what they were chanting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were chanting "Yugoslavia," they were singing the national anthem, and they were asking for freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That can be heard from the clip, the masses chanting "Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nice said to you yesterday that this group, as he called it, sent various demonstrators to different places. Who was it that was sending different people to different places?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about these groups and these demonstrators. I never had any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice indicated that it was I who sent them to different places. I'm going to read something out to you now from what Mr. Nice submitted yesterday. This is an interview by Mr. Solevic. That is page 03641691. In the paragraph on the left. I'm not going to read the whole thing. The question is: "You started with Vojvodina. "Miroslav Solevic: Yes. Those attacks started from Vojvodina." He's talking about attacks from Vojvodina, attacks against Serbs in Kosovo. "They were biting." You remember, after all, you were at that meeting in Kosovo Polje in 1998 when -- 1988, when we decided to go. Milomir Minic and Dragan Nikolic came from Serbia. This is Milomir Minic and Dragan Nikolic who were party officials; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
