utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says, "Now you should ask them what kind of positions they had then. "Question: They were quite perplexed. We have to stop." This is what he whispered to Minic. "Minic, perspiring: Try that. "Solevic: Exactly. I got up at this meeting and I said, please, there will be no more bargaining here. No one should come to see us any more. Now we are going to go to light a fire underneath the windows of those who are against us." This is the interview given by Mr. Nice, provided by Mr. Nice. This is an interview with Miroslav Solevic but provided by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that put to the witness yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. Oh, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the position it's in the original Serbian newspaper or B/C/S newspaper but not translated because, of course, we have to be selective in what is translated but I have no objection, providing it's capable of being dealt with by the Court and that it should be dealt with in this way because otherwise the accused can't take the benefit of a document that's put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, then let it be put on the ELMO so it can be translated for our benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's 10th of February version in B/C/S. Last footage it is 1691 ERN number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said whether the witness was shown this, Mr. Robinson, I don't mean whether what I am quoting was shown the witness but whether the article was shown the witness, and it was. But what was quoted wasn't what I can see in the article. It's talking about the meeting, and in the hall Minic tells me, Have you gone mad? and then I whispered to him, Don't you worry about that. And then the subtitle is What Milosevic nonsense that you -- it says that it was rumoured that you agreed upon everything with Milosevic and that it was all construed. Bosic said What Milosevic, nonsense. We did everything on our own bat. The only problem was how we should go, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Solevic himself in this interview says not only did I not send them, but he says heaven forbid. We did that for ourselves. Is that what you know happened? Is that how you know it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended numerous meetings in Kosovo Polje. This conversation between him and Minic is something I'm not aware of, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the conversation but who sent the people there and did they go and did anybody send them at all outside Kosovo or was it their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian and Montenegrin people, the Serbs and Montenegrins who found themselves enmeshed in this drama of massive exodus and everything else that accompanied it decided for themselves and then went around the towns of Serbia to tell the people what was happening, what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija and what was happening to the Serbs and Montenegrins, to inform them of the situation and to ask them for help to save Serbdom in Kosovo and Metohija, to save the Serbs and Montenegrins in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As Solevic says, the attacks started from Vojvodina, they kept stinging us by what they said, and then you went there - not you but the citizens - went there to hold a rally because of these attacks that were hurled at them from Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At their own initiative without any orders from Belgrade or instructions from Belgrade. Not only to Novi Sad but other towns all over Serbia. There were invitations coming from these Serbian towns to come and hold rallies there, and there was even a rally that was held in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Skopje, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you were asked by Mr. Nice, since he mentioned a million people at Gazimestan, he asked you whether this was risky business because there were many Albanians living in Kosovo, and you said no, that it was not a risk. Do you remember, Mr. Balevic, in view of the fact that there was this enormous mass of people gathered there, whether there was a single incident that broke out throughout the whole day, the entire day, the arrivals, the departures, the presence of all those people at Gazimestan, did a spark fly at all? Did an incident take place? Was anybody hurt or injured or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single incident, untoward incident took place either before -- before the arrival or from the railway station to the rally itself, in the cars, before the meeting, after the meeting. No incidents ever broke out. Otherwise I would know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the demonstrations that took place in 1988 and throughout that year. Mr. Nice yesterday used a term "the demonstrators used violence or force." Do you know whether at any demonstrations throughout that year anywhere whether there was any violence at all?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Except where there was destruction if you're talking about the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the demonstrations that you were asked about by Mr. Nice when the Serbs went to complain and present their grievances.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any violence in all those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because he said the demonstrators used force or violence.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said there were 300 armed Serbs as well in front of the cultural centre and that's not true either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you explain this to me now, please: You mentioned, in speaking of the meeting attended by the people you enumerated, you said Gorica Gajevic, Milomir Minic, Dragan Tomic, the other Dragan Tomic, Sainovic, et cetera. That's the order you gave us for the names. Now, was this a meeting of the Main Board of Kosovo and Metohija, the meeting of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Kosovo and Metohija, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting, as far as I remember, of an expanded nature with more members. I wasn't a member of the board. I was there as secretary. But it was an extended meeting of the members of Kosovo and Metohija, the members of the Main Board, the provincial board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was an expanded meeting, an enlarged meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that means that all the provincial board members were there plus all of you others who had some posts and functions, which means that it was a meeting, if you say that the Main Board was there and that other representatives of the Socialist Party were there, does that mean that all these functionaries were there, officials were there as leaders in the Main Board of the Socialist Party?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, and I answered Mr. Nice's question and said that they were there on behalf of the Main Board of the SPS, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Nice showed you many people standing at the railway station in Pristina or where else. Well, in Kosovo at any rate. Many people near the border. And he quoted from a document. I assume it was the Human Rights Watch or something like that, I can't quite remember now, but he quoted from a document in which it said that there were armed policemen standing round them. Now, since I didn't see any armed policemen on the photographs and images that were shown, any armed police encircling those refugees, and I that if a foreign television station took that footage that must have been something that would have been seen, did you see anywhere in Pristina any armed policemen forcing the Albanians to go to the railway station and move out?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that before, and I'm saying it again: I never saw that. I said yesterday -- I told you yesterday about the bandits and crimes committed by criminals and so on. I'm not claiming that there might not have been people who would don the uniform of a policeman and abuse that uniform, because the KLA had many police uniforms, too, so they might have done that. I don't say that there wasn't any abuse of that kind, but as far as the regular police force is concerned and regular policemen forcing people out, I have no knowledge about that in the area of Pristina in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice went on to quote a tragic event from that book, that is that in Kosovo Polje the house and a clinic of an Albanian doctor was stormed and people slaughtered there, as he said. He said this was done by the policemen and soldiers. Tell me, please, you said you knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, had an incident like that happened, a massacre like that happened, could that be hidden from the people? Would you have to have known about that by virtue of your function?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible that anything like that could have happened without my knowledge. That's the first point. Secondly, I had my daughters living there, I had friends living there, and I lived in Kosovo Polje myself in 1980, so it was impossible for a massacre of that kind to have taken place without me knowing about it in one way or another because I was and inhabitant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you hear of any crime committed by an army unit or a police unit, anything like that? As a unit. I'm not talking about sporadic incidents, individuals. Many individuals were arrested for the various crimes they committed, but do you have any knowledge about any kind of even the smallest unit of an army or a police force perpetrating a crime and killing any civilians?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I claim with full responsibility that I never had any information telling me that even the smallest military or police unit had perpetrated crimes against the Albanian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice mentioned various paramilitary formations as well. Now, you in Pristina, and you were there throughout the time of the crisis and the war, did you happen to see any paramilitary formation whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Balevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson, may I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Vladislav Jovanovic. Yesterday and today, I came here in court with a raised temperature because I got out of bed and I had a temperature. So might I suggest that I start the examination-in-chief of Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic on Monday, the next working day apart from tomorrow so that I could have a chance to go back to bed and deal with my temperature, because I have had a temperature on both days and I had to get out of bed. So I don't -- if possible, as it's going to be a lengthy witness and I won't be able to get through him tomorrow, might I be allowed to start my examination-in-chief on Monday or the next working day after tomorrow, not tomorrow, and be allowed to rest tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a temperature now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I took two Paracetamols. Perhaps it has gone down now but this morning it was 37.8, and yesterday the nurse took my temperature at her own initiative when I returned from the courtroom and it was above 37 degrees Centigrade. I didn't ask her to take my temperature, she did so herself, because I thought that I should continue and get -- but I don't feel too well. So I don't think I can start the next witness today or tomorrow. The witness is prepared, but I think for practical purposes, if I was allowed to get well now, that would save perhaps a little more lengthy recuperation period later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we deal with that, I have one question for Mr. Balevic before he completes his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm confused, Mr. Balevic, about where you were living at the various stages of the matters which have been explored in examination and cross-examination. Can you tell me when you lived in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Kosovo Polje from the 3rd of January, 1961, until somewhere towards the end of 1980. I can't give you the exact day, but that's the period. And then I moved to Pristina. I had a flat -- I mean, I lived in Pristina, resided in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's until recently?

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there until I was expelled by the Albanian terrorists, forced to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me of the date of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th I left Pristina, because my security was threatened, with my family. I went to Kosovo Polje to stay with my daughter. And then on the 26th, I left Kosovo Polje, in June 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you were there from the 26th of March until -- you were there from the 26th of March, 1999, until June 1999. In Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MITAR BALEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo Polje, I was there from the 19th of June to the 26th of May -- no, June. June, sorry. June. Because on the 19th of June I left Kosovo for Pristina, went to stay with my daughter, and Kosovo Polje -- I was in Kosovo Polje for seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Balevic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to testify. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw your -- I'd like to draw the attention of the interpreters that their conversation is being picked up by the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sure they'll thank you for that, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This point give rise, I think, to two issues: One, whether this is now a stage in the trial where assigned counsel should be in a position to step in and take the witness in chief. We understand the witness has been prepared, and if assigned counsel is not in a position to do that, then it's hard to see when he's going to be able to fulfil his full role. If the decision is against that, then the next question that arises, and it was I think was forecast some time ago, is whether time that is lost through ill health comes off eventually the time allocation for the accused's case. The rationale for all of that is that the accused's pattern of ill health, which we saw last year and which we now see somewhat reflected in what's happened last week and this, may be a pattern that is connected to the amount of work he's doing on running this case at his own choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he just had the flu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that was last week he had flu. And that happened also last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Last year he had other --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he had other things as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- conditions, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small addition. The whole floor has the flu where I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's going around, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in terms of practicability, do you think is it possible or feasible for the assigned counsel to take up the conduct of trial right now or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know what the relation is between the assigned counsel and the accused, but it might be tomorrow. And of course, if it was tomorrow and if the courtroom was available, it might be that we could use some other part of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the assigned counsel is allowed to meet the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And this witness, incidentally, is a witness who speaks fluent English, as I understand it, and no doubt would have been very fully prepared and will know exactly topics that are going to be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And his examination will not complete by tomorrow. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We understand, I think, six and a half hours have been allowed, so that will take us to the end of an ordinary sitting week in any event. And I should say, for the assistance of Your Honours at the moment, that I have in mind a plan to make cross-examination of the witness easier by, with your leave, serving on the witness all the documents I want him to consider for the Prosecution between the time roughly when his examination-in-chief ends and his cross-examination begins. That's the plan I've laid at the moment. But in any event, yes, he could be taken in chief starting tomorrow and we could perhaps finish him if not on Thursday, if there was a court available on Friday, otherwise next Monday. But flu or not -- and I don't think we've seen a medical report ourselves, and make no complaint about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was a medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently we have seen one, it has come our way, sorry, it just hasn't found its way to me yet. But flu or not, there is a pattern in these things and the Court made the decision it did about assigned counsel with that in mind. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect to Mr. Nice, this is an extreme application. This is an application that is not based on merit by him. He should consider this application very carefully. It's a very dangerous thing to start building up a so-called pattern against the accused when he has genuine illness which may afflict anyone. It's the time of year when it is. Medical reports have been filed with the Court that establish the genuineness of his condition, completely unrelated to his underlying medical condition relating to his cardiovascular problems, and in his position at the moment, it is to his credit, in our submission, that he came to court yesterday, participated in the proceedings fully, and also did today rather than hold up these proceedings. In our submission, that shows a genuine desire to assist this Court. Any proceedings where an accused is struck down by flu, has a temperature and is unwell, are at risk of being disrupted, and it can happen to any of us. And in our submission it would be wholly wrong for the Court at this stage, with such an important witness lined up to be heard over many hours with which the accused has undertaken a considerable amount of research, it would be wholly wrong for his medical condition, which is one that can afflict anyone, to be respected [sic]. And in our submission, the Court should understand his position and resume, as he requests, the proceedings on the Monday. That would be a normal and reasonable approach. To start putting this forward as some sort of pattern I think can lead this Court into grave error in the way of viewing this accused. We know from the medical report that this is completely unrelated to the previous issue which afflicted him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is what we'll do: We'll one spend the rest of today's session dealing with the legal arguments relating to the -- that evidential issue. Mr. Milosevic, you should be examined by the doctor this afternoon when you return, and at the end of the day we'll decide, having received the medical report on your condition. You may leave now if you -- if you wish. I mean, Mr. Kay can deal with the legal arguments, if that is your wish, or you may stay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, I cannot accept anything being done here without my presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So sorry. Have Your Honours had an opportunity of looking at the materials we provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we have not received them yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I thought they ... I hoped that they would have found their way to you a little earlier, but ... Now I've mislaid mine. There are three decision, and Mr. Kay and Ms. Higgins, I know, have provided a couple of others. As I explained, first instance decisions have gone both ways. If necessary and if helpful, we can, now that perhaps there's a little more time today possibly make a full collection of what we know of first instance decisions as well, but here are two Appeals Chamber decisions and one first instance decision. The first Appeals Chamber's decision in Brdjanin and Talic is in respect of the subpoena for a journalist to attend, and the first flag is on page 3 at paragraph 4, simply sets out the relevant background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wonder if I can interrupt. I'm speaking for myself, I know, but I find it very difficult to deal with the relevance of an authority to a legal issue without first of all identifying what the proposition is that you're advancing. Now, my principal concern in all this, and I think it probably is the principal concern of all of us, is whether things become somehow or other part of the Prosecution case in the Defence phase, albeit they are not somehow or other accepted by a witness in the course of cross-examination. Now, is there anything on that topic in any of these authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you help first of all by telling me what the proposition is that you're advancing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm sorry if I jumped to an assumption that we were working on the same topic. We picked up, really, where we left off yesterday, but our proposition is that the materials that have been laid before the witness, and in particular the two newspaper articles and the extracts from Death of Yugoslavia, are materials that can properly be before the Chamber for the two reasons I advanced yesterday: One, that they are in themselves capable of being evidence of the truth of the things said because they are, even if a speech is of hearsay, and documents tend to be hearsay, they nevertheless qualify under the Tribunal's rules of admissibility. And secondly, they may qualify because they touch on questions of credibility of a witness. And so that the -- that's the underlying proposition. And it's with that in mind that the Brdjanin case summary at paragraph 4 will be of assistance. "Brdjanin was charged with a 12-count indictment with, among other things, crimes against humanity and grave breaches..." Next sentence: "The Prosecution sought to have the article admitted into evidence, claiming it was relevant to establishing that the accused possessed the intent required for several of the crimes charged." The article is an article of the Washington Post. "The Defence objected on several grounds including that the statements attributed to Brdjanin were not accurately reported. The Defence stated that, if the article were admitted, they would seek to examine the appellant so as to call into question the accuracy of the quotations noted above." Now, it may be that with Your Honour's particularly articulated concern we ought to go back to find out a little bit more about the procedure. So if we come back to paragraph 2: "The appeal concerns a subpoena issued by Trial Chamber II to compel the testimony of a war correspondent concerning an interview he conducted while reporting on the conflict in the former Yugoslavia." This is at page 2, paragraph 2. "The appellant --" that's this -- the person, the subject of the subpoena -- "served as a correspondent for the Washington Post in Yugoslavia. On the 11th of February, 1993, the Washington Post carried a story by the appellant containing quoted statements attributed to Radoslav Brdjanin, one of the accused, about the situation in Banja Luka and the surrounding areas. The article described Brdjanin as a 'housing administrator' and 'avowed radical Serb nationalist.' He was quoted as saying that 'those unwilling to defend (Bosnian Serb territory) must be moved out' so as 'to create an ethnically clean space through voluntary movement.' According to the article, Brdjanin said ..." various things attributed to him. And then we came to the summary on paragraph 4. Paragraph 5 -- sorry, I perhaps should complete paragraph 4. "The Defence objected on several grounds, including that the statements attributed to Brdjanin were not accurately reported ... stated that, if the article were admitted, they would seek to examine the appellant so as to call into question the accuracy of the quotations noted above. The Prosecution then requested that the Trial Chamber issue a subpoena to the appellant, and the Trial Chamber complied on the 29th of January." Dates in February and March the subpoena was discussed, and, "At these sessions the Prosecution informed the Trial Chamber that the appellant had refused to comply with the subpoena. And on the 9th of May, the appellant filed a written motion to set aside the subpoena. On the same day, the Prosecution filed its response." And the Trial Chamber heard oral argument on the motion. "Refusing to recognise a testimonial privilege for journalists when no issue of protecting confidential sources was involved, the Trial Chamber upheld the subpoena, and it also found that the article was admissible." So that here we -- although the overall hearing is concerned with the compulsion of the witness, this part of the appeal jurisprudence deals with the admissibility of such an article. And if we can then turn to page 16 and to paragraph 50. Perhaps -- it says this: "In view of the foregoing, the Appeals Chamber holds that in order for a Trial Chamber to issue a subpoena to a war correspondent a two-pronged test must be satisfied. First, the petitioning party must demonstrate that the evidence sought is of direct and important value in determining a core issue in the case. Second, it must demonstrate that the evidence sought cannot reasonably be obtained elsewhere. "Finally, the Appeals Chamber will not address the submissions of the parties on the second ground of the appeal, that is, the application of the proper legal test of the facts. Having determined the principles governing the testimony of war correspondents before the International Tribunal, the Appeals Chamber considers that it is the role of the Trial Chamber to apply these principles in the particular circumstances of the case. The Appeals Chamber would, however, offer the following observations. "First, contrary to the Trial Chamber's apparent fear, even if the Trial Chamber were to decide that the appellant should not be subpoenaed to testify, that need not mean that the article must be excluded (and the Prosecution disadvantaged to that extent). The admissibility of the article depends principally on its probative value under Rule 89(C) and the balance between that probative value and its potential to undermine the fairness of the trial under Rule 89(D). Because the article is hearsay, the Trial Chamber will also want to examine what indicia of reliability or unreliability it carries." And that refers to a decision of this Chamber in Kordic and Cerkez on the statement of a deceased witness. "As with many pieces of hearsay evidence, the inability of a party to challenge its accuracy by cross-examining the declarant (in this case the appellant) does not mean that it must be excluded. Rather, that inability would diminish the confidence the Trial Chamber could have in its accuracy and thus the weight the Trial Chamber would give it. "At the same time, and contrary to the Trial Chamber's apparent counterbalancing fear, admitting the article without subpoenaing the appellant need not prejudice the accused. The Defence may still question the article's accuracy, and the Trial Chamber will have to take account of the unavailability of the appellant in determining how much weight to give the article. "Finally, whatever evidentiary value the article may have, it is the Trial Chamber's task to determine whether the appellant's testimony itself will be of direct and important value to determining a core issue in the case. The Defence has offered two justifications for seeking the appellant's testimony. The first is that his testimony will enable the Defence to challenge the accuracy of the statements attributed to Brdjanin in the article. The second is that the appellant may place Brdjanin's statements in a context that will cast them in a more favourable light ... With regard in particular to the first justification - concerning accuracy - given that the appellant speaks no Serbo-Croatian and thus that he relied on another journalist for interpretation, the Appeals Chamber finds it difficult to imagine how the appellant's testimony could be of direct and important value to determining a core issue in the case. In any event, determining whether the appellant's testimony on either score may Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have direct and important value to a core issue in the case requires a factual determination that is properly left to the Trial Chamber. "Therefore, should the Prosecution ... still desire that the appellant be subpoenaed to testify before the International Tribunal it will have to submit a new application..." Thus, then, the Appeals Chamber decision on the approach or an approach to be taken to a newspaper article. And that brings us in a two-stage process to His Honour Judge Bonomy's particularly articulated concern dealt with persuasively, not authoritatively in the Appeals Chamber sitting on appeal from the ICTR in the following case of Rutaganda decided by a Court comprising His Honour Judge Meron, Judge Pocar, Jorda, Shahabuddeen and Guney, a judgement rendered on the 26th of May of 2003. And if Your Honours would go to, as it appears here, page 9 of 13, under heading C, Cross-examination of Rutaganda Using Collateral Documents. "The appellant submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law by allowing the Prosecution to use three non-disclosed documents during his cross-examination. The documents at issue are pictures taken from a book in the ICTR library, an Agence France Press newspaper clipping, and the articles of the Association of Radio Television Libre Mille Collines showing the initial shareholders. The appellant argues that as these documents were not disclosed during the Prosecution case, the Prosecution was effectively permitted to split its case. In addition, according to the appellant, the documents were admitted as hearsay evidence without any inquiry being made as to their reliability. "Lastly, the appellant argues that the Trial Chamber failed to apply the principle of equality of arms. In support of this submission, the appellant cites a specific example to show that a different standard was imposed on him. The appellant concludes that the prejudice suffered calls for a retrial. "The Prosecution submits that the arguments are baseless, contends that the documents, deemed relevant to the cross-examination by the Trial Chamber, were not subject to disclosure and no prejudice was suffered by the appellant through the use of the documents. "The record shows that the start of the cross-examination -- at the start of the cross-examination of the appellant, the Prosecution presented the Chamber with a file containing documents that it intended to use during cross-examination. The three documents cited by the appellant were also within the file, and had not been previously disclosed to the Defence. The Trial Chamber permitted the Prosecution to tender them, but, in order to allow the appellant time to familiarise himself with the materials, postponed questioning on them until the following day." Pausing there, the practice of providing cross-examination documents ahead of cross-examination may have been particular to that Chamber at the time. The presentation of the documents in this cross-examination in the course of the giving evidence will not, I think -- will not, I respectfully submit, change matters of principle at all. Paragraph 283: "The issue the Appeals Chamber must first settle is whether, given that the materials had not been previously disclosed in conformity with Rule 66 or 68 of the Rules, the Trial Chamber erred by allowing the Prosecution to use the materials during the cross-examination and, if so, whether this error is such as to invalidate the judgement. "Considering that the photographs, the press clipping and the articles of Association of RTLM bordered on issues that had been raised by the appellant during examination-in-chief, the Appeals Chamber considers that the Trial Chamber had the discretion to admit them during cross-examination of the appellant. Moreover, the documents in question were not documents the Prosecution was required to disclose under Rule 66(A) or permit the inspection thereof under Rule 66(B) of the Rules. Since the documents did not seem to be of an exculpatory nature for the appellant, the Prosecution was under no obligation to disclose them to the appellant under Rule 68 of the Rules. The allegation by the appellant that the Prosecution did not discharge its burden of disclosure is thus unsubstantiated. "The appellant contests the use and admission of photographs taken from a publication entitled Rwanda, les medias du genocide. The nine photographs show the Interahamwe at an allegedly peaceful demonstration in support of the Nzanzimana government, various Rwandan personalities including the then president ..., 'moto taxis', the appellant wearing an MRND cap and the appellant and the Interahamwe at the MRND extraordinary congress held in July 1993. The record shows that the Prosecution indicated during the trial that it obtained the publication from the ICTR library for use in the cross-examination of the appellant. 'The trial record shows that during the examination-in-chief, the appellant also spoke of the 'moto taxis,' referred to as the 'Interahamwe taxi', and of his attempt to initiate with others the holding of a possible Interahamwe za MRND congress, which was subsequently relegated behind the MRND party congress. In addition, the appellant indicated during his examination that he wore an MRND hat when he attended meetings and that he had participated in MRND rallies; and throughout his examination, the appellant spoke generally about the structure, activities and purpose of the Interahamwe za MRND. "Therefore, in the opinion of the Appeals Chamber, the appellant has not demonstrated that the Trial Chamber erred by admitting the photographs contained in the publication entitled Rwanda, les medias du genocide -" means of genocide - "which would afford the Prosecution the opportunity to rebut the allegations made by the appellant during his cross-examination. In any event, were it established that the photographs should not have been admitted, the Appeals Chamber would still be of the opinion that the appellant had not demonstrated that he suffered any prejudice by their admission or that they had an impact on the judgement. "As regards the AFP clipping dated the 14th of May 1994 and relating to statements ascribed to Robert Kajuga, chairman of the Interahamwe za MRND, and the articles of Association of RTLM with the list of initial shareholders, the Appeals Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber had the inherent discretion to admit them. "In seeking to have the documents admitted prior to cross-examination, the Prosecution contended that it intended to use them in response to matters raised during the appellant's examination-in-chief. The record supports this argument. The appellant testified about Robert Kajuga in the course of his examination, and stated that he never heard anything discriminatory from Kajuga. Likewise, concerning RTLM, during his examination-in-chief, the appellant testified about his investment in the station and gave details and names of other shareholders. "The Appeals Chamber finds, therefore, that it has not been established that the Trial Chamber erred in admitting the press clipping and the articles of Association of RTLM. "It should be recalled that the Trial Chamber accorded the appellant sufficient time to familiarise himself with the photographs, the press clipping and the articles of Association. However, counsel for the appellant did not avail herself of the opportunity to re-examine the appellant on the photographs or on the articles of Association. Notwithstanding, during cross-examination by the Prosecution on the photographs, the Presiding Judge indicated that the author's comments should be treated with caution. As regards the press clipping, the Appeals Chamber notes that the appellant called into question the authorship of the article and underscored that the statements contained therein were attributable solely to the chairman of the Interahamwe. The appellant has not shown that the Trial Chamber failed to consider these factors when admitting the materials and when assessing their impact on his testimony. "Lastly, the Appeals Chamber notes that the appellant has not put forward any convincing argument to show that the documents were unreliable or that the Trial Chamber violated the doctrine of equality of arms." And thus dismisses the arguments of the appellant that the Trial Chamber erred in law by the admission of the documents at that stage. Your Honours, because I hadn't been able to make the documents available to you -- these judgements available in advance, I took you through the passages in full. And in my submission, we have here two authorities going to show the admissibility in principle of a newspaper article of the kind that has been put before the last witness, or indeed of the clips from the film or television documentary The Death of Yugoslavia, and that the judgement from the Appeals Chamber sitting for the ICTR shows that for these documents to be presented to a witness in cross-examination is an entirely proper course to take where issues arise in the way that they have arisen in this case, in many ways parallel to that in the case under appeal. I was going to turn to the last authority but I see Your Honour has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is what were the facts of this case? I'm concerned in particular about paragraph 287. The Appeals Chamber even conclude that even if there was some error in admitting the material, it didn't have any impact on their judgement, which is at first sight an odd comment but that there might be an explanation for that. But what were the allegations that the appellant was making which were being rebutted by using this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The full detail of those, if you're going to sit over the break, may be something to which I would prefer to return, but Your Honour's drawing to my attention that particular paragraph, the first question Your Honour raised, I think is identifying a reality of these cases, particularly in light of recent Appeals Chamber rulings, and that is that there has to be articulated judgements identifying routes to decisions that Trial Chambers make. And therefore, if documents are admitted such as the documents that were admitted here or as documents that we would ask you to admit through this witness, but in the event they form no part of the decision-making process and therefore no part of the actual judgement, why then it can properly be argued that the Chamber has put them out of its mind and in the event not relied upon them. And that's -- I think I mentioned earlier I was, with great respect to the Appeals Chamber, dealing with the issue when it arose in front of this Chamber differently constituted for the dead witness. I was always sad that I hadn't persuaded an acceptance of the material on the basis that the Trial Chamber would not have relied upon it without more material on the basis that it wouldn't have relied upon it on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm directing attention to that paragraph because I think, unless you can indicate otherwise, I think that contains the rationale for the decision, and the rationale for the decision seems to be that it won't do any harm. I mean it's a negative rationale. It doesn't give a positive basis for allowing prosecution material to be admitted during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure but perhaps we better find out a little bit more about the allegations which in the time since yesterday I haven't done. But I'm not sure that's the rationale, because it says, "The appellant has not demonstrated that they erred by admitting the photographs contained in the publication which would afford the Prosecution the opportunity to rebut the allegations made by the appellant during his cross-examination." So that in principle, the documents are there to rebut allegations made and that is parallel to the purpose for which I wish to put, for example, some of the newspaper articles to this witness when he speaks in the terms he does of the overall purpose of the meetings in April 1987 and the participation in them by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that, though, it constitutes an innovation on ordinary adversarial procedure. I don't see this at the moment as an issue over the admissibility of hearsay. That doesn't seem to me to be the problem. The problem is to do with the order in which the case is said in the Rules to be presented. And indeed am I not right in thinking that so far as the Prosecution case is concerned, this material would have had to be disclosed at an earlier stage, whereas because it comes in somehow or other in the course of cross-examination you are exempt from the rules that would otherwise apply to you in presenting your case-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to disclosure, I think the position with the material -- well, the material subject to our application to have exhibits produced, is similar to that in the Rwanda Tribunal but different in part. As to the newspaper articles, and I'll find out in due course when we first had them available to us, unless they contained Rule 68 -- a Rule 68 element, then they would not have been material we would have been any duty to disclose. Would Your Honour just give me one minute. Ms. Dicklich confirms that which I thought, and that is that the newspaper articles, so far as I'm aware, and it's difficult to say this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with absolute confidence given the holdings of material we do have here, that they had not been in our possession until very recently, probably in the course of the time the witness was giving evidence, because it became obvious to us that it might be relevant at that stage. Different considerations of course apply in relation to The Death of Yugoslavia because that material was made available to the accused in various forms, I think, right at the beginning of the trial and has been supplemented to some degree by being provided with the full interview, records of the various contributors, or some of the contributors in any event, since then. But -- so whether there was a duty of disclosure in respect of The Death of Yugoslavia tape in whole or part, it's in fact been available and, once more, it's a sort of publicly available document. As to the newspaper articles that we looked at yesterday, they fall broadly within the same category of documents dealt with here in the ICTR case save for the fact that we didn't actually have them until very recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I'm making a broader point, Mr. Nice, rather than one confined to the particular facts of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the ordinary course under Rule 65 bis there is a scheme for intimation of witnesses and exhibits, and in the course of preparing your Prosecution case, you would normally have to submit a list of all the exhibits you'll be using in the Prosecution case, and somehow or other this case that you're referring to from Rwanda gets the Prosecution round all that because they happen to be introducing the material in the course of cross-examination. Now, you may then justify the late introduction on various grounds. I follow that and that's a point you've just mind, but they're not dealing with that. They're saying as a matter of principle it doesn't matter when you find the stuff you can put it in, and that's what I find rather odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not seeking to raise an argument against myself, we can put it in subject, of course, to the proper exercise of discretion by the Court to exclude it. But the decision of the Appeals Chamber, it may be, reflects an understanding of the realities of trials like this which are subject to this, it may be, defining characteristic that there is no possibility for identifying a closed field of evidence relating to any of these large cases, either at the beginning, the middle, or the end of the case. And inevitably, more material comes to the Prosecution, becomes available to the Prosecution -- when it comes to that, is probably available daily to the Prosecution given the access that the Internet provides to sources of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is material that is put to a witness to contradict him in cross-examination subject to the general rule of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, not knowing in advance what a Defence witness list is going to look like, there's no way it could be. And in any event, as a matter of principle I don't believe -- I would invite you to say it isn't subject to part of the regime. And of course, even outside the complex cases we deal with here, back in an ordinary domestic trial in an ordinary domestic jurisdiction, if a witness turns up and says something that the prosecutor understands can be contradicted by a new document to which he -- for which he searches as a result of what the witness says, he can typically and without difficulty raise it in cross-examination, because there's no way he can be criticised for doing so. If a Defence witness turns up and says something that he's contradicted in an earlier statement and the Prosecutor finds the statement, or if he says something that can be contradicted by and is material and satisfies all the rules, and can be contradicted by rebuttal evidence, then of course that can be done. What we see in these trials is that small reality more easily articulated by rules and regulations. What we see is that reality but written on a very large scale, because these cases are very large and the issues they raise are always --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I turn to another aspect? As far as the news article is concerned, the issue we have at this moment is whether to admit a newspaper article written by a third party or interview of a third party which the witness did not accept and which was not dealt with with the witness in the examination-in-chief. The appeals case, two cases we have, we've been just provided, is dealing with some other -- the case is a bit different. Take the ICTR decision. I draw your attention to paragraph 289. It's a news article regarding Mr. Robert Kajuga. But that was dealt with in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we don't have this kind of case. In Brdjanin the case was about the accused or the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respectfully differ from the one -- from the characterisation of the evidence here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the -- I'll just find my copy of it. Because the issues that the newspaper -- thank you very much. The issues that the newspapers cover are indeed issues that this witness had explored -- had explored through him by his evidence in chief, because I used earlier this morning and yesterday the motion of broadening of a case without any complaint about the accused, and what's happened here is it may be an example of something that's going to happen recurringly. The -- we opened the case in respect of this meeting shortly, and although I haven't got the words immediately in front of me, I can recall them and we can find them from the opening note. It was suggested by me in opening that this encounter where the words "You will not be beaten" were used was an event that either reflected or created or stimulated the accused's interest in the pursuit of power. I'll get the exact words shortly. We approached the meeting on that basis without going into a great deal more detail about it, but we identified this as a very important date, and a date of course to which we will be taking the Chamber in due course when seeking to establish and identify the accused's state of mind both at the time of the commission of the crimes as alleged, a state of mind that will be built on or fed by or explained by the state of mind that he has on his rise -- or had on his rise to power. The accused witness takes the same event that we've characterised in the alternative way that we did and presents it in a different way, in an entirely favourable light for the accused. We then have from Solevic, a man with whom the witness was undoubtedly -- with whom he was undoubtedly connected in some ways at the time. We've heard his evidence on that. We've had first the account of the 1985 meeting. Well, the witness knew nothing of that. We then on the first article had an account of the visits to Kosovo Polje, which the witness broadly accepted, I think, and before we come to the second article, we have the analysis by Milosevic of being an instrument of the accused's power. Well, now, that does fit with the very way we've put our case and is contrary to the very much more favourable way these events were described by the witness. And coming back to the first part of the article, the reference to the meeting in 1985 that Solevic said was refused him, that again feeds, supports the interpretation of events that may be made of the meeting in April in 1987; was this an awakening of an interest or stimulation of an interest rather than feeding on an earlier interest. When we come to the second article, the article of the 10th of February -- time may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was wondering whether we would endeavour to finish now, but I think perhaps it would be better take the break, unless -- Mr. Kay, how long would you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can see it being at least -- I can see it being at least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll take the break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I also want to get the facts of the case and we need to break for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can help you with Rutaganda. The photographs were some of which the accused were in. The articles of the RTLM radio station, the accused had invested in RTLM, he was an investor, put money in. And the newspaper clip comments by Robert Kajuga, he was the chairman of the Interahamwe, the accused had said when giving evidence that Kajuga had never said anything discriminatory, and so it was to counterpoise what he had said then in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You would suggest these are all different from showing clips of other people that might have been witnesses here expressing what they think happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We heard what Judge Kwon said and what Your Honour, I think, has already said about the connectivity of this material, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, wouldn't it be far more logical, in the interest of the truth, if all of this is that important to call Mr. Solevic as a witness? You're going to spend more time here to prove what happened in Rwanda, as Mr. Kay was explaining now and Mr. Nice explained for almost an hour here, rather than having Mr. Solevic testify. There is no logic in this. It goes against common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, authorities have been cited. It's an important legal issue. We have to consider them. But I remind you that you may -- we will excuse you if you do not wish to return after the 20-minute break, which we will now take. We're adjourned for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I conclude what I have to say about the article and then return to the additional material we've got in answer to His Honour Judge Bonomy's request. That perhaps will be the most orderly way of dealing with things. The second article of the 10th of February, we only looked at a couple of passages of it, mostly for want of time, but the passages we looked at shows two things: Solevic making it quite clear that the rallies in Novi Sad and, by inference, subsequent ones started and brought down the leaderships of Vojvodina and Montenegro and were planned to bring down the leadership in Bosnia until they were stopped by the accused. That is, of course, contrary, absolutely contrary to some of the very recent evidence today of the witness. The following passage that's been translated dealt with the circumstances in which the group of which in one way or another and to whatever extent the Chamber may decide the witness was aware broke up and, as is described here, was brought to an end by the accused. The passages on The Death of Yugoslavia tape include passages that the witness effectively adopts because they were put in not on a selective basis, the whole passage in that video recording was covered subject to removal of editorial comment, so that he was able to adopt and make a point for re-examination by the accused out of Stambolic saying that Stambolic sent the accused to Kosovo, but of course he disagrees with what Solevic was saying about the use of stones and matters of that sort. With those summaries in mind, the only additional material on fact that we've been able to obtain about the facts in the Rutaganda case and to which in particular paragraph 288, the AFP clipping, relates - and I've told what I've learnt to Mr. Kay and he with knowledge of the case because he was, I think, in Rwanda at the time and therefore has some knowledge of it, was able to explain his understanding of it, which I think makes complete sense. What we learn is that the statements ascribed to Kajuga in the article relate to the Interahamwe's support of the civil defence in the fight against RPF, the killing of RPF infiltrators as well as innocent civilians at roadblocks and incidents with the Red Cross and its ambulances. And so putting that together with what we find in paragraph 289, it would appear that the appellant testified that Kajuga never said anything discriminatory, that the AFP clipping revealed Kajuga saying things that, although it doesn't absolutely appear from the summary I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have, were capable of being interpreted as discriminatory. And, Your Honours, in our respectful submission, what you have here is, of course, not exactly parallel because it's an entirely different issue, but of similar validity. I can tell you, incidentally, exactly how I opened this part of the case because it was -- What I said of this was that the incident -- I said this: "To what extent if any that incident --" That's the you-will-not-be-beaten incident. "To what extent if any that incident was stimulated and planned matters little. It was that phrase, 'You will not be beaten' and the response to others to it that gave this accused the taste or a better taste of power, maybe the first realisation of a dream. It gave him an opening." And so it was clear the Prosecution's case was that whether he already had ambition and a taste for power, this added to it. Alternatively, it was a first taste, and it gave him an opening. And that's within the overall thesis of the Prosecution, that this accused's driving force was never other than his own pursuit of and retention of power, not backed by a philosophy or other ideology. Now, with that in mind, when the witness gave the account he did of how it all happened and how there could be no question of the accused reflecting a nationalism in any way, the matters said by Solevic in the newspaper articles and by Solevic and to some extent others on the video clip become admissible because they are relevant and they have some probative value, and there is no ground for there being excluded, in our respectful submission. They come before you without these witnesses having been summoned to be part of the Prosecution's case, a point that I think His Honour Judge Kwon had in mind at one stage, for a range of reasons but principally because the way we presented the case, and at that stage it wasn't necessary or essential to go beyond the way that I had summarised it, and it is the accused who has responded to that in the way that he has. I repeat yet again: No complaints of that. But in light of the way we presented it in a case where there was always going to be severe limitations on the number of witnesses we called, the particular people here identified were either dead, as in the case of Stambolic, there's another man called Pavlovic, the man who was dismissed by the Communist Party following this meeting and figures significantly. The television director, he's also dead. Of those who are alive, we made applications for Vllasi, and I must correct the explanation I gave yesterday because my memory of the history was wrong, but in the event it turned out not to be possible even to apply to call him for want of time in reality. And the other one is potentially Solevic, but there is very little reason to think that he would have been available to us at that stage of the case even if he might be now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you tell me what the difference in principle is between asking for a document or a video to be presented at this stage as part of your case and asking to interpose a witness, Solevic, for example, at this stage? What is the difference in principle?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the difference in principle, or is it the difference in effect? And I'm not avoiding Your Honour's question. The difference in principle is that at this stage, the material - query whether it becomes evidence - the material serves a purpose of putting the finder of fact on notice that such material exists and possibly, depending on all the other circumstances, giving it some weight. So, for example, to go back to the domestic trial, the small domestic trial, the Defence witness comes and gives evidence, the prosecutor discovers late that there is a statement, whether in a newspaper or some other way, having some indicia of reliability, he puts the statement to the witness and the witness hedges his bets and says something about adopting the statement but doesn't adopt it in full. The statement may in those circumstances have some real weight. Alternatively, the witness denies the statement completely. At that stage, it may be that the material would have no weight until and unless it is formally proved at a rebuttal stage in the case. So that my analysis would be first that it's -- I can see why Your Honour asks the question, but there is a difference, I think, in principle because if I put it in as part of my case, it would go in straight away for the truth of its content, however -- however great or small that might be. So that if, for example, the witness concerned today, supposing we wanted to put in something of what the -- of what Mr. Stambolic says, for example, and we know, of course, his book's already gone in in parts with other witnesses, but we want to put in something with Mr. Stambolic. We apply to do it in chief in our case, we get leave to put it in, it becomes evidence straight away. We put it in in cross-examination for a particular purpose, depending on the reaction of the witness to it, depending on what the Chamber thinks about it, it either becomes immediately some evidence of the truth or it becomes notice that there may be further evidence to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I think is a particularly good example. You got lucky because the witness died. He would never think of offering him as your bit of cross-examination material, but you've got his statement because he's dead, so you offer it. You see, all you would be able to do in respect of a witness is say, "Well, I have information" - you don't necessarily need to say from where - put it to the witness, and if he agrees with it you've got it as part of your case because he's accepted it. If he disagrees with it there's no way you can deal with it unless the rules allow you to bring along this witness at some other stage in the case, for rebuttal or whatever. Now why in principle is it different if you've got a document rather than a witness? Because all these documents are doing is telling you what the witness has said. They're basically -- they're basically witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are indeed similar to witness statements. They have one different character, namely, that they've been available publicly for some period of time, but that apart, no, they're very similar. But they nevertheless exist as things, whereas witness statements, generally speaking, are not admitted. I mean, I could put one in or I could seek to put one in but you probably wouldn't be very interested in looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But they are here. Now, this actually brings us -- something else I was going to raise -- to a real stark reality and problem of this case, and probably all these cases. Witnesses such as the last witness may be witnesses who are never going to change from a position that they adopt. They may always be very black and white witnesses. It may happen on both sides. We had an example of this with early Albanian witnesses, I think, who the Chamber may remember denied the existence of KLA in their villages, matters of that sort, for some time. Now, the Chamber may want to ask itself this question: If the evidence of this witness, expanding or developing the accused's case as the accused is entitled to do, was simply challenged by me with the substance of all these newspaper articles and I simply put propositions to the witness, as sure as can be he would say no to all of them. We know that. That's the reality of this type of trial. You wouldn't understand why I was making those assertions. You wouldn't have seen the material. You wouldn't know that it puts you on notice that his answers may be wrong, that his credibility may really be an issue. But once I present you with either, A, Solevic saying in terms that things are different from the way the witness describes them, or newspapers articles of people speaking saying that things are different from the way the witness describes them, is not the Chamber better informed and better able to start the process of assessing the credibility of the witness and the underlying facts? And of course is not the Chamber far better equipped to know whether at the stage of application for rebuttal evidence, which it can foresee coming, and/or when it decides whether to call any witnesses itself, how to exercise its various discretions. And that then brings me to this general point: The desire to fit these trials into tight rules is understandable but may not be realistic. These are cases where the maximum of material, in our respectful submission, is likely to lead to the best conclusion. And it's interesting to note that the accused - and it's his trial, it's not Mr. Kay's trial - never seeks to exclude material. He's always happy to deal with it. And today isn't the only example. There have been other such examples. He's happy to deal with it. He doesn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not opposed to the accused bringing in hundreds of thousands of pages in favour of his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't say that, Your Honour, and I would be for several reasons and it would depend on the documents. But we were actually by no means particularly vigorous in our opposition to documents he sought to produce. Some we did, but not particularly. We raised the issue and left it to the Chamber to decide but we were not particularly difficult about that. And for reasons I've already given. There may be reasons for imposing a different test on the first stage of the trial from that where a Defence is bound to be forthcoming from the second where a rebuttal case is only a possibility. But we have -- I was also interested, if I may say so, perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, bear in mind Mr. Kay has about 30 minutes, and the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Last point, then. The need for a full exploration of materials in line with what I suspect civil systems might do was perhaps revealed by His Honour Judge Robinson's question to me this morning: Was I suggesting that there may have been planning between the first and second meetings which could have led to violence. Well, now, if in the ordinary process of asking questions I have not yet sufficiently described the Prosecution's view of the culture and society with which you're dealing so that that wouldn't have been clear, then either I've failed or the system fails, for of course we will be advancing that the culture in which this meeting occurred and the culture in which this accused rose to power was one in which people could be injured by stones, much, much worse, we may ultimately discover, could be contemplated and effected. And a narrow application of admissibility rules is going to run the real risk of the Chamber misunderstanding. A broad approach recognising that matters can be dealt with in judgement by exclusion and by limiting the effect of material that isn't otherwise supported will safeguard the fairness of the trial without allowing the Chamber the risk of simply misunderstanding the history. So this material, in our respectful submission, informs the Chamber about this witness and about the surrounding circumstances and should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue we're dealing with here concerns the use of material in cross-examination, not to prevent it being used in cross-examination but its status, having been used, whether it goes on to become an exhibit in the case. That is the issue that we're dealing with here, and there is a great distinction between the presentation of material in cross-examination and then its introduction, having gone through a series of questions with a witness, that makes it become an exhibit in the case. We've made a series of objections over the last few months over the use of material by the Prosecution because it's been our position that documents are being presented in a routine and wholesale way as a matter of practice and technique that do not derive themselves from the Prosecution exhibits or the Court exhibits or Defence exhibits but are new materials which the Prosecution is seeking to introduce as further exhibits in the case in support of their case regardless as to whether the witness, who is supposedly the instrument by which they're being introduced into evidence, regardless of whether he adopts them or not. So the Trial Chamber is faced with these pieces of paper moving across the courtroom not being adopted and not having any status. It is not even an issue of hearsay, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, in the cases cited by Mr. Nice, was there any discussion of the question of the adoption by the witness of the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. These cases have all concerned, in fact largely, other than the one point concerning the Kajuga statements, these cases have concerned issues concerning the accused himself. In Rutaganda, he was in some of the photographs. Some of the photographs had the taxis which the Interahamwe went around Rwanda within to demonstrate a particular point. The articles of the RTLM radio station, he'd been an investor in that particular enterprise. So there was a connectivity between him and the material. And the Kajuga issue arose as a result of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something he had said in his evidence in chief which obviously reflected upon his state of mind and went directly to him, and it was an issue of that accused's credibility. The Talic case, again, was a newspaper interview allegedly given by the accused making certain assertions that the Prosecution wanted to introduce. The Defence produced a very technical attempt, I think something more prone to use in American courts where the particular advocate came from, over the authenticity of that and that it hadn't been proven by the Prosecution because it wasn't accepted by them. In a lot of jurisdictions, that could have been introduced as a previous inconsistent statement to impeach the witness and go to his credibility. And one can see, in fact, no objection to the technique sought to be used by such a statement. We're not -- sorry, My Lord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt but to keep the flow, Mr. Kay, can you say whether, or tell me from your recollection, whether in Rutaganda it could be argued that the material or any of the material might have been used by the Prosecution in support of their case without somehow or other being acknowledged by the witness or accepted to some extent, whether any of it was freestanding, in other words, like all the material in the present case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This material, the Appeals Chamber didn't think much of it one reads from the ultimate decision, so I don't think they put much weight to the particular document. So we don't have a greater amount of information. But I think it arose because of an attack on the accused's own credibility and his state of mind. And he was charged with genocide. The particular allegations were that he had been instigating the genocide and he had been driving others to commit the acts during the hundred days of the conflict in Rwanda, and it was how he gave his evidence. That's really what the issue was -- was looking at, and he had made statements about Kajuga which the Prosecution obviously wanted to attack to show his own state of mind. So it was very particular, in my submission, to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can look at the Trial Chamber judgement, I take it, and find the basic factual position, so please don't spend time on it if it's not something that's absolutely clear in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's not that, but I just echo that state of mind issue is how I read it. We're here, of course, dealing with something entirely different. And it's not just three documents in Rutaganda or one document in Talic. It is a wholesale process and an advocate's technique in developing their case through what we would describe as the back door, and this is what we have been alert to in the last few months and why we have been making our objections on a regular basis, and I think why the Trial Chamber may now be considering the issue as a whole, because what happens is if the witness adopts some of the fact, a pretty minor fact it maybe, that there were 150.000 people at a demonstration, the whole article appears to be going in in evidence, with all its comment, all its point of views, and all its statements, when it's not formed any part of the material from that witness. And the technique that's being used here is a continuing development of the Prosecution case on matters that were not raised in their own case through their own witnesses, thereby giving the accused an opportunity to challenge and cross-examine. If one is dealing with only a few documents in the course of a trial we don't really have any particular problem and we go -- the Judges are very easily able to deal with the issue of weight and how important and significant that material is, but we're getting to a stage here where in any judgement of this Trial Chamber there are masses of potentially amounts of documents being put in by the Prosecution that you're going to have to deal with and say, "Well, we don't attribute much weight to that because of this, because of that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the 150.000 number was the only item that the witness adopted, you would then say that would not be a sufficient basis to have the document put in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. It because completely irrelevant and nugatory. There is no point in having that, just getting the witness to confirm a fact - Gazimestan was on a particular date - and the document goes in, but not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that the Trial Chamber, if it were exhibited, could attach what weight it wished to such a document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why do you -- why do you need it? Because it's in evidence from his mouth that that was the figure. The document isn't needed. And when we're talking about widening this case, this is happening through these documents at a pretty alarming rate. And I think if the Trial Chamber permits this technique, you're going to see, as in the 89(F) issue that we had during the Prosecution phase of the case, wholesale material coming in that you're going to have to deal with. So it's an important issue of principle here for the future running of the trial. Any decision made now may give an opportunity for the Prosecution to run with the baton and run wholesale with its evidence through the Defence phase of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there any question of unfairness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does that arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've got it with Solevic. The accused is saying, well, call him let's hear what he has to say. No one is able to question him here. We see edited clips from a TV programme which turns out is carrying a very misleading translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber confronted that issue in one of the cases cited and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With respect, the Appeals Chamber was dealing with it on a very limited basis of three documents in Rutaganda. They weren't dealing with the matters of principle. If I could refer the Court to a transcript we've obtained from the Hadzihasanovic trial, 29th of November, because this is a -- it seems to us, certainly from the Defence bar at this Tribunal, this is an ongoing policy this Court is being faced with in relation to what is going on here. There's another trial that has experienced this as a problem, and that Trial Chamber had to deal with it.
