We've been able to get the transcript out this morning, and if I can just put copies before Your Honours now. The Prosecution have been given one earlier. It's Judge Antonetti in the Hadzihasanovic trial, transcript page 12521 to 28. Looking at the first page, the Defence counsel made an oral motion on new documents being used in the course of cross-examination after the presentation of the Prosecution case. And the Trial Chamber requested information on the source of the documents, where they were obtained, and the circumstances by which they came by them. Second page, "The reason for this debate between the parties is that the Prosecution produced documents they hadn't requested to be tendered into evidence when presenting their case, and they did so in the course of examining witnesses for the Defence." The Prosecution said that they had provided the documents in support of the allegations in the indictment, and it was as a result of certain Defence issues. The foot of page 2, the Judge refers to Kupreskic. "The Defence responded that the Prosecution had the burden of proof and that it should not produce new documents in order to protect itself in the light of arguments presented by the Defence." And they say that the rules governing cross-examination don't really deal with the details of it. The Court goes through disclosure under Rule 65 ter (iii), which Judge Bonomy has referred to this morning, the issue of rebuttal that has also been referred to, and credibility. The issue that the Court deals with then on page 3 is that, firstly, one is exempt from this Rule if the Prosecution believes that the credibility of a witness could be brought into question; and secondly, the second exception concerns cases where the Prosecution wants to present a document in order to refresh a witness's memory. We're dealing here with presentation, not admission as exhibits, which is a different issue. The Court went on at line 14 on page 3 to say: "The Trial Chamber would like to indicate that there is a principle which is fundamental and which must be respected by the Prosecution, and that is that the Prosecution must present all its evidence in the course of its case." And they cite Kunarac, which we have here, where that principle is affirmed that the moment for dealing with the Prosecution case producing evidence is largely during their phase when they are proving the indictment. The next case -- the next page: "As a result of this principle, the Prosecution can only present in the course of its cross-examination of a witness new documents that have not been admitted -- it may present new documents only if it wants to reinforce evidence that it has presented already or if it wants to introduce new elements that concern the criminal responsibility of the accused."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These rather open the door, do they not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I think one has to go through further to see where they -- where they end up. If we go to the foot of that page, at line 22: "The Prosecution may make such request in the rebuttal stage, and pursuant to Rule 85(A)(iii)..." and we know that in accordance with the manner for tendering documents into evidence as it comes about from the Celebici judgement. Secondly, it may request that a case be reopened if it wants to deal with new evidence. Again, Celebici. The Trial Chamber points out that the Rule concerning cross-examination is limited to the various points that are stated within the Rule and then goes on to say, "The scope of cross-examination of a witness by the Prosecution -" I'm at line 19 - "is thus limited to the points referred to in 90(H) of the Rules. In the course of such cross-examination, the Prosecution may naturally confront the witness or may present to the witness any documents that have already been admitted into evidence." No issue there. "The Prosecution may present and request certain documents to be tendered into evidence, if these documents have not already been admitted into evidence, in the course of cross-examination, but the conditions will be much more restricted and will be governed by the principles that have already been referred to. "In the opinion of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution may present, in the course of its cross-examination, any documents that have not already been admitted in order to test the credibility of a witness or to refresh such a witness's memory." It goes on to say: "... the Prosecution may present a document not already admitted and which it has had in its possession before... "The Trial Chamber is of the opinion that when the Prosecution plans to present such a document in the course of its preparatory work, they must disclose it," and they say within 24 hours. Line 16: "The Prosecution may request the admission into evidence of a document that it has disclosed provided that it is in order to establish the credibility of a witness or to refresh a witness's memory. And such document can only be admitted in a limited manner and can only be used to establish credibility of the oral testimony of the witness or to refresh the witness's memory." This is a translation from French into English, and in my submission, the issue of credibility there is the one of a previous inconsistent statement of that witness where he has said something else and that witness's own credibility is an issue. If these newspaper articles had contained a statement from Mr. Balevic in which he had said something inconsistent, then classically that could go in and could be an exhibit as it was an issue concerning his credibility. But what we're having here is the Prosecution attempting to use the procedure to confront the credibility of the witness and establish the credibility of someone else whom we haven't heard from and we don't know whether in fact they accept or adopt that statement and whether it was reported correctly. He can be cross-examined on that line, but the material should not go into evidence as an exhibit. That is a different status entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what if you do have the example of a prior inconsistent statement but the witness denies making it? How do you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it is put to him, the circumstances have to be dealt with properly as to when it was made, justified, and the evidence goes in, the Prosecution in their rebuttal case may call the journalist or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the party who received the statement to affirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's still got to be established at some stage if there is a dispute about its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have had a significant change in the law in my home jurisdiction this year and from the 2003 act on consistent -- inconsistent statements out of court. Juries used to always be directed, well, it's what the witness says in court that's more important than what they said before. That rule is gone now and in fact the court takes -- the courts have to direct juries in a much more sensible way; well, it's a matter for you. That is capable of being evidence just as much as the evidence on oath. So it's a matter that you must decide upon, having looked at the overall demeanour, credibility of the witness, and the circumstances of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But presumably that is after a police officer who took the statement has given evidence to confirm that that is in fact what was said if you're faced with a denial by the witness of ever having said what's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can go down that route or you don't have to go down that route, but I'm not saying that any material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- that is an inconsistent statement is incapable of being an exhibit. Given the rules -- if I can make it clear, my submission is that any statement by the witness, consistent or inconsistent, by the accused, consistent or inconsistent, a Defence exhibit, Court exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit, is all capable of going in and being put into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 53 of the Appeals Chamber's decision in Brdjanin and Talic, it says: "At the same time and contrary to the Trial Chamber's apparent counterbalancing fear, admitting the article without subpoenaing the appellant need not prejudice the accused. Defence may still question the article's accuracy, and the Trial Chamber will have to take account of the unavailability of the appellant in determining how much weight to give the article."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That accords with my submission that I've just made, remembering that this was a statement of the accused and so obviously has a relevance and probative value. But the issue we're dealing with, of course, is statements of other people not on the same matter of principal. So we're not attempting to exclude anything that would be material from the witness or the defendant at all. We're not putting technical rules on this. Our concern is statements made by other people out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just finally, Mr. Kay, at the top of the fourth page, which you did say might be made clear later, the Trial Chamber here seemed to be recognising the consequence of what they describe as a principle. The principle is the order in which the respective cases are presented. But it says, "The Prosecution can only present in the course of its cross-examination of a witness new documents that have not been admitted only if it wants to reinforce evidence that it has presented already or if it wants to introduce new elements that concern the criminal responsibility of the accused." Now, if that's right, that allows for a wide-ranging introduction of documents in the course of a cross-examination of Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the word "present," it's not "admitted." And the Judge, as I said, in the later, next two pages, makes a distinction between presenting, the test, and then admission. And of course Mr. Nice can say, well, what about this, and he has a statement from someone and cross-examine, but if it leads nowhere, it shouldn't become an exhibit. He can -- as long as he's within Rule 90(H)(i) in the conduct of his cross-examination, which is the subject matter of the evidence in chief, credibility, unable to give relevant evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think if you read earlier parts "present" means become part of the evidence. If you read the previous page the use of the verb "present" seems to imply that it's becoming evidence in the case. And while I follow all the other propositions you've advanced, I find difficulty with that passage at the top of the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I can't help you any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to point out, too, that to the extent that it is a question of stage and phase, the rule in 85 is residual in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The rule as to the stages, unless otherwise directed by the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But let us see whether the accused has something to say. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Mr. Robinson. What Mr. Nice requested has nothing to do with this witness. Therefore, to introduce evidence through a witness, documents that have nothing to do with that witness, seem to me -- seems to me to be beyond all reason. And secondly, in this sea of procedural arguments that have been put forward and which are mostly based on some Rwanda experience, in this specific case I think is -- has completely stepped -- forgotten a notorious fact with respect to what Mr. Nice wishes to prove. During the testimony of Mr. Balevic, during his examination-in-chief, I showed you a document from the Federal Ministry of the Interior, the commission that worked at the time in that far-off year 1987, from which you can see that the police used force against citizens unjustifiably and not that it was the citizens which caused the police's reaction. And this was established by the federal commission that was set up. So doesn't it seem to you to be absurd for Mr. Nice to try and prove here that this was something that was organised in advance, for me allegedly to have to intervene? Then I would have had to organise this among the police ranks, which as you know at that time was mostly the Albanian police at the time, that they should attack the citizens so that the citizens should flee and that everything should happen that ensued. That is absurd. Secondly, Solevic, in what I heard from these excerpts that were shown, confirms that, precisely confirms that; that they were attacked and that they fled and that they came to that pile of whatever it was that they started throwing at them. So he explained that, and his statement, therefore, is not contradictory to what Balevic said. And then finally, I also told you that if that is so important, then it would be logical to call Solevic to testify and explain what he meant. We can't have these explanations coming from Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice can't explain some events that took place in a completely different context and mechanically to attach them and clip and paste them onto something else. That is untenable. And also I would like to draw your attention to one more point and it is this: We're talking here about several levels of quality and weight for some documents. I assume that an authentic footage of an event has -- carries weight in one form rather than post festum what somebody thought about this, did, or anything else. So you can weigh up the weight of the evidence. You had authentic footage here that was discussed by Mr. Nice but any person of reason would be able to draw their own conclusions for that. They don't need interpretations five or ten years later whether something happened this way or that way. So I think there's a hierarchy of levels of importance that are being presented. Otherwise, any material evidence or authentic footage is material evidence and could be refuted by somebody's statement later on, because somebody might say they didn't like it, or that it was different, it happened in a different way. So I don't think that is at all acceptable. And finally, as you can see, it is I who take up least time here. I don't take up a lot of your time, but you can check this out. Has this binder with the exhibits been introduced into evidence, the documents I put forward during the Balevic examination with the footage from the Aco Marovic school and in front of the cultural centre, the speech at Gazimestan, the stenogram of the meetings in the Aco Marovic centre or hall, and many other documents. The report by the federal secretary for internal affairs about the incident that took place. So you have a whole pile of documents and exhibits which we attach to the testimony of this witness and the witness confirmed them, and I'd like to tender them into evidence and I'd like them to be introduced if they haven't been introduced already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll deal with that matter later, Mr. Milosevic. We are beyond the time now for the adjournment. As I indicated earlier, we are expecting a medical report this afternoon. The court Registrar will intervene in that matter and we'll issue an order later in the day as to the resumption of the trial. Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only to say that the first instance decision at the end of the clip of documents we provided - we didn't have time to go into it - but you may find it helpful, and I adopt many of the points made in the document supplied by my learned friend Mr. Kay. And nothing else. Except maybe this: The Chamber may, in looking at the problem in the whole, because we may have to come back to it, be assisted by contemplating the 65 ter summary for the witness that's just gone and addressing or addressing the problems that face preparation for witnesses for whom we have summaries of this kind at some stage. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Kunarac decision that I referred to has been made available. Shall we pass it through your clerk to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you very much. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned sine die
